summary: Make sure aria-disabled buttons use a consistent focus style
_description:
Splitting this out from #66038.
See comment at https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13390/#issuecomment-6061122370

Now that Core is going to use more and more the pattern already used on Gutenberg where disabled controls use `aria-disabled="true"` instead of a `disabled` attribute, the styles that come from buttons.css, colors.css, and potentially other stylesheets should be adapted to ensure the aria-disabled buttons get a consistent focus style.

Reminder: using `aria-disabled="true"`:
- Helps making controle discoverable, for better general usability.
- Helps preventing focus losses when controls are disabled, as they are still focusable.

summary: Administration: Replace Dashicons icon font with @wordpress/icons SVG components in wp-admin
_description:
== Problem / Current Behavior ==

The WordPress admin area (wp-admin) still relies on Dashicons, an icon font introduced in WordPress 3.8 (released December 12, 2013 — over 12 years ago). While Dashicons served WordPress well, the icon font approach has significant limitations:

 * '''Inconsistency''': The block editor and Site Editor already use `@wordpress/icons` (SVG-based React components), while the rest of wp-admin uses the legacy Dashicons font. This creates a visual and technical split within the same application.
 * '''Performance''': The entire icon font (~300+ glyphs) is loaded, regardless of how many icons a page actually uses. This adds unnecessary weight to every admin page load.
 * '''Accessibility''':
   * '''Screen readers''': Icons may be read as nonsense or ignored entirely, confusing users who rely on assistive technology.
   * '''Font overrides''': Users who change fonts for readability can break all icons, turning them into empty squares.
   * '''Copy-paste''': Copying text that includes icons produces random, meaningless characters.
   * '''High-contrast mode''': Icons can vanish when users enable high-contrast or forced-colors settings in their OS.
   * '''No built-in meaning''': Icon fonts are just styled characters with no inherent description — accessibility has to be added manually.5.5. No new icons can be added.

== Proposed Enhancement ==

Replace Dashicons icon font usage in wp-admin with `@wordpress/icons` SVG components (or inline SVGs derived from the same library). This would:

 1. Unify the icon system across all of WordPress, block editor, Site Editor, and classic admin screens would all use the same modern icon library.
 2. Enable tree-shaking so that only the icons actually used on a given page are loaded.
 3. Improve accessibility: inline SVGs support `aria-label` for example.
 4. Allow new icons to be added as needed without growing a monolithic font file.


== Rationale ==

This is not a new idea, it has been the stated direction of the WordPress project since 2020:

 * The [https://make.wordpress.org/design/2020/04/20/next-steps-for-dashicons/ Make/Design blog post] (April 2020) confirmed Dashicons was closed to new requests and that future efforts would focus on the new Icon component.
 * [ticket:49913] explicitly states: "This update is the final planned update of the Dashicons font. Moving forward, the more modern approach of using SVG icons directly (as the block editor currently does) will be explored."
 * [ticket:47498] comments reference "a long standing plan to remove all font icons from core in favor of SVGs."

Six years have passed since this direction was set, and no formal ticket tracks the actual migration work. This ticket aims to formalize the effort and track progress.

== Backward Compatibility ==

This is a critical consideration. Many plugins and themes use `dashicons-*` CSS classes for admin menus, meta boxes, and custom UI. A migration plan should:

 * Maintain the `dashicons` stylesheet as a deprecated fallback for a defined transition period (multiple major releases).
 * Provide a compatibility layer so that existing `dashicons-*` class references continue to render correctly, perhaps by mapping them to their SVG equivalents.
 * Document the migration path for plugin and theme developers with clear timelines.

== Related Tickets / References ==

 * [ticket:49913] — Final Dashicons update (WordPress 5.5)
 * [ticket:47498] — Checkbox/radio SVG migration, discusses removing font icons from Core
 * [ticket:41074] — Dashicons 4.9–5.2, discusses SVG direction for the admin
 * [https://make.wordpress.org/design/2020/04/20/next-steps-for-dashicons/ Next steps for Dashicons] — Make/Design official post
 * [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/07/15/dashicons-in-wordpress-5-5-the-final-update/ Dashicons in WordPress 5.5: The Final Update] — Dev note
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/icons @wordpress/icons package on GitHub]

Combining characters aren't normalized to Unicode Form C on output
_description:
The HTML produced by WordPress functions like `get_the_excerpt()` and `the_content()` doesn't perform any Unicode Normalization.

This lack of normalisation is problematic because the W3C recommends Normalization Form C - https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm/

It is possible to wrap these functions - for example `normalizer_normalize( get_the_excerpt(), Normalizer::FORM_C );` - but this quickly becomes cumbersome in complex themes.

Would it make sense for WordPress to ensure that the content coming out of the post object is normalized before being returned?

**Test**

My blog post contains the text `Anaïs`. The `ï` is U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I and U+0308 COMBINING DIAERESIS.

When I run the output of `the_content()` through the W3C Validator, it complains

> Warning: Text run is not in Unicode Normalization Form C. 


**Background**

There's this previous ticket which talks about normalizing in the editor and on save - #30130.

However, for anyone saving plain text / markdown this doesn't seem to work. Text is saved un-normalised.

summary: Tests: Reduce the cost of the heaviest PHPUnit test classes
_description:
#65887 gave the suite its first published timing data and closed. This ticket is where the follow-up work lives: the classes that cost the most, claimed one at a time.

== What we can measure now ==

 * [63410] publishes six aggregate metrics to CodeVitals after every push to trunk: main suite time, p95 and p99 per-test time, maximum test time, and counts of tests over 500 ms and over 1 s. https://codevitals.run/public/WordPress/wordpress-develop/metrics
 * [63412] annotates any test over one second on pull request and trunk runs, with a summary table naming the slowest tests.

The first two trunk data points on August 31 were 443 s and 330 s for consecutive commits that touched no test, so single points are noise on shared runners. Only a sustained shift means anything. The same two runs counted 32 and 20 tests over one second.

== Where the time is ==

One local run of trunk at 6c0f205fd6 on August 16 (PHP 8.3, MySQL 9.7, Docker, single site) gives the shape. Directional, not authoritative:

 * 30,865 tests in 1,066 classes, 234 s of summed per-test time.
 * '''Half of that time is in 22 classes.''' A quarter is in 7.
 * 61 REST API classes account for 49% of it.

The heaviest classes by summed time, in seconds:

||= sec =||= tests =||= avg =||= class =||
|| 16.3 || 197 || 0.083 || `WP_Test_REST_Attachments_Controller` ||
|| 11.8 || 281 || 0.042 || `WP_Test_REST_Posts_Controller` ||
|| 7.0 || 151 || 0.046 || `WP_Test_REST_Post_Meta_Fields` ||
|| 6.9 || 200 || 0.034 || `WP_Test_REST_Comments_Controller` ||
|| 6.9 || 259 || 0.027 || `Tests_REST_API` ||
|| 6.5 || 359 || 0.018 || `Tests_Media` ||
|| 6.4 || 452 || 0.014 || `Tests_Blocks_registerCoreBlockStyleHandles` ||
|| 5.2 || 129 || 0.041 || `WP_Test_REST_Users_Controller` ||
|| 4.9 || 113 || 0.043 || `Tests_Image_Functions` ||
|| 4.6 || 11 || 0.421 || `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` ||
|| 4.5 || 93 || 0.049 || `Tests_Theme` ||
|| 4.4 || 4,474 || 0.001 || `Tests_WpTokenMap` ||
|| 4.3 || 95 || 0.045 || `WP_Test_REST_Themes_Controller` ||
|| 4.3 || 848 || 0.005 || `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` ||
|| 3.8 || 100 || 0.038 || `Tests_REST_WpRestUrlDetailsController` ||
|| 3.8 || 129 || 0.030 || `Tests_REST_Server` ||
|| 3.4 || 29 || 0.117 || `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` ||
|| 3.2 || 95 || 0.033 || `WP_REST_Global_Styles_Controller_Test` ||
|| 2.7 || 70 || 0.039 || `WP_Test_REST_Tags_Controller` ||
|| 2.6 || 49 || 0.054 || `Tests_REST_WpRestTemplatesController` ||

Two profiles appear, and they need different fixes. `Tests_WpTokenMap` and `Tests_Canonical_PostStatus` are data-provider matrices of cheap tests, so the lever is the size of the matrix. `Tests_Admin_ExportWp` and `Tests_Image_Editor_Imagick` are a few expensive tests, so the lever is fixture and I/O cost inside each one.

== How to work a class ==

 1. Claim it in a comment here, one class at a time.
 2. Measure before: `npm run test:php -- --filter Class_Name`, then read the `time` attributes in `tests/phpunit/build/logs/junit.xml`.
 3. Apply the levers the handbook already documents: hoist immutable fixtures into `wpSetUpBeforeClass()`, share expensive objects across the class, trim provider matrices that exercise identical code paths, and mock file or image work where the assertion does not need the real thing.
 4. Measure after, the same way, and post both numbers on this ticket with the PR.

Guardrails: no assertion is removed to save time, no expected value changes to make a test pass, no timeouts are raised, and a test that protects a specific behavior stays even if it is slow.

Related: #42904, #42278 and #41451 (older performance proposals that can now be evaluated against data), #63026 (the bcrypt precedent), #52645, #65887.

summary: Fix DOM and visual order mismatch in the various media dialogs
_description:
In the various media dialog, the buttons in the top toolbar come first in the DOM order but they are visually placed after the main dialog heading on the left.

This introduces a mismatch between the DOM order and visual order that is an accessibility barrier for screen reader users. Note that this has nothing to do with Tab keyboard navigation. Rather, it's about navigating content with arrows keys or other screen readers navigation mechanisms (e.g. 'read all').

Worth also noting that any other software will get the order mismatch, including AI agents.

For example in the Media Library 'Edit attachments' modal dialog, the `edit-media-header` element, which contains the 3 buttons Previous, Next, and Close, comes before the `media-frame-title` element, which contains the H1 heading. As such, when navigating content following the DOM source there is a mismatch between the DOM and the visual order.

Same in the media dialog, where the `media-modal-close` button is before the H1 heading in the DOM.

It's also worth noting that now that initial focus is set on the modal dialog element, there is no need for the buttons to be the first thing within the dialog.

Grunt: Add a stylelint precommit task to check for CSS syntax errors
_description:
We need to do a better job of catching sad syntax errors and problems in our CSS before commit - things like parse errors, empty rules, units on zero values, and possibly duplicate properties (when alone, not as a part of a group). There may also be a thing or two that we could enforce per our own standards, such as requiring a comment to follow any declaration with `!important`.

CSSLint seems to do most of these, provided we turn off the majority of its checks. Many of those checks (vendor prefixes, selector specificity, etc.) either are not relevant to our set up (due to Autoprefixer, for example) or are just not feasible given our current CSS and possibly not desirable for this project.

Interested to know if there are any other tools out there that perhaps fit the job better, and defining the parameters of what we would like to check.

summary: Multiple select elements associated with tables in the admin (filters, user role changes) lack visible, persistent labels
_description:
Throughout the admin, there are select elements that have labels hidden with screen reader text and that rely on the default or first option in the select to provide a visible label. Here is an example, filters for the posts table: {{{
}}} [https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/13153456/489316152-9127bf2b-5112-4412-aaf8-e8bd9f808670.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..4XjPhUl9Pd0j6RNRjS9_oGBSrhPjsQXlymtPScsM_SE See image of post filters missing visible lables.] Other places that this technique has been used include: * Bulk actions select * Change user role select * Media filters * Comment filters [https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/labels-or-instructions.html WCAG 3.3.2: Labels or Instructions (Level A)] requires that labels or instructions be provided when content requires user input. This is generally interpreted to require visible and persistent labels. In the current implementation, once a user has selected an option in the select, there is no longer a visible label for the select. It is posisble for users to link directly to filtered versions of these tables which would pre-fill the select with a date or category, for example, in which case any user following that link would not have access to the label for the select. It is worth noting that to receive the accessibility-ready tag for a theme, we require all inputs and form fields to have visible and persistent labels. This technique in the admin would fail an accessibility ready review were it followed in a theme. In addition, these fields also fail [https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/label-in-name 2.5.3: Label in Name (Level A)], as the visible text for the first option (or any selected option) does not match the label. Example: The hidden accessible name for the date filter select is "Filter by date" and the visible text is "All dates" or any selected date, such as "August 2025". This mismatch between the visible text and the label would make it difficult for users who rely on voice control to interact with these fields. The admin UI should be reworked so that selects have visible labels that don't rely on the default option in the select.

summary: Block Supports: Add PHP helpers for generating styles and classes when serialization is skipped
_description:
This ticket tracks backporting changes from Gutenberg to WordPress Core.

Gutenberg PRs:
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84207
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84205
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84208
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84206
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84209

It adds a PHP helper for each of the border, shadow, spacing, color and background block supports, wp_get_border_classes_and_styles() and so on, mirroring the JS getBorderClassesAndStyles() family. Each takes block attributes and returns the support's class and style. The block supports now build their output with these helpers, and blocks that skip serialization can use them instead of rebuilding styles by hand.

Avatar, Post Featured Image, Icon, Post Navigation Link, Navigation Submenu, Comment Author Avatar, Calendar and Button currently copy parts of this logic, and the copies have drifted. Those blocks move onto the helpers when the Gutenberg package is next updated.

This is a behaviour-preserving change, so the block support output should be identical to before. It depends on https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/13491 (background clip) landing first.

summary: Many PHPUnit tests are not well isolated
_description:
In talking about tests at WCUS 2026, we reminded ourselves that many of our PHPUnit tests leak state and/or depend on previously leaked state. This is easy to see by running the tests in an arbitrary order:

{{{
npm run test:php -- --order-by=random
}}}

This lack of isolation can result in varied problems:
* A test cannot be run by itself
* A test class cannot be run by itself
* A test passes because of some previously leaked state and not because the test is actually testing the correct thing
* etc.

Reducing state leaking reduces fragility, increases confidence that tests are testing what they should be testing, and is a likely prerequisite for future parallel test running.

This ticket is for sharing a grab-bag of unrelated test fixes we worked on during WCUS.

summary: Tests: Let WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase reflect read-only routes
_description:
Follow-up to #40538, splitting out the structural half so it can land on its own.

== The problem ==

`WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase` declares nine abstract methods (`tests/phpunit/includes/testcase-rest-controller.php`, lines 24–40 on trunk today):

{{{
test_register_routes()   test_context_param()    test_get_items()
test_get_item()          test_create_item()      test_update_item()
test_delete_item()       test_prepare_item()     test_get_item_schema()
}}}

Every controller test must implement all nine. A read-only controller has no create, update or delete route, so those three methods have nothing to assert. Since [53921] and [54058] the accepted way out has been `@doesNotPerformAssertions`, with the note that it "can be reconsidered in the future".

That has not stayed flat. Trunk today carries 101 `@doesNotPerformAssertions` annotations in 26 files, and 98 of them are REST controller tests. Twenty files sit under `tests/phpunit/tests/rest-api/`, plus three under `fonts/font-library/`, two under `icons/`, and one unrelated case in `user/passwordHash.php`. Each new read-only controller inherits the pattern on the day it is written.

== Options ==

 1. '''Default implementations that assert the negative.''' Make the six operation methods non-abstract, with a default that dispatches the operation against the controller's collection and item routes and asserts it is rejected (`rest_no_route`, or the controller's documented error). A controller that supports the operation overrides the method as today. This turns 98 no-ops into real assertions with one change and no per-file work, and it stops the count growing.
 2. '''A read-only base class.''' A second testcase with the read-side methods only, and controllers pick the one that fits. Cleaner signature, but every existing read-only controller test has to move, and nothing stops a future controller extending the wrong one.
 3. '''Leave the abstract alone''' and keep annotating. The status quo.

Option 1 seems the best trade, but the default needs care: some controllers register a route and reject the method with 403 or 405 rather than `rest_no_route`, and the schema for a POST body differs per controller. A first patch could dispatch and accept any error response, then tighten.

Once the base class change lands, the remaining annotations outside the abstract methods are a per-case read, which stays on #40538.

Related: #40538, #41463, #55652, [53921], [54058].

summary: REST API: Preserve boolean values when generating next/prev Link headers
get_routes() called multiple times within single REST request causing the rest_endpoints() filter to also fire more than once
_description:
Hi all,

Many thanks for creating the REST API, and also for getting it into core! :)

When I had a closer look at how to integrate this in our projects I noticed something peculiar with the rest_endpoints() filter: it is called multiple times over; in some cases twice, in others three times.

So I did a little digging around and found that the root cause seemed to be the use of get_routes() at multiple locations:
- in the rest_pre_dispatch filter (rest_handle_options_request)
- in the rest_post_dispatch filter (rest_send_allow_header)
- in the dispatch() itself
- in the get_index() method
- in the get_namespace_index() method

After looking how these locations interact with each other, I couldn't detect any code which altered the generated route map between consecutive calls to get_routes().

I will add a patch in which I propose to store the generated route map in the class, and re-use that one instead of generating yet again the same array (and also re-filtering the same array).

Since the name 'endpoints' is already taken, and being used in the initialization as well, I thought it would be prune to use another variable name: $route_map, which is also being used in the current doc-block.

I did not profile this patch (not really sure how to do that), so I'm not sure if storing this rather large associative array is a good thing to do. However generating it multiple times (and re-filtering it also) may also be quite 'expensive'.

Thanks,
Ruud

summary: Users with "same" email address can be accidentally created
_description:
Wordpress does not permit multiple users with the same email address, using RFC 5321 to define the localpart of the address.
However, several major email service providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) ignore mixed case in localparts.
This means that WordPress will support 2 users with email addresses abc@gmail.com and ABc@gmail.com - although those 2 addresses represent the same mailbox.
Propose an enhancement:
  1. Warn admins when manually creating a user that the new email address might be a duplicate of...
  2. Highlight email addresses on the admin Users page that are case-insensitive identical.

summary: Disable sizes=”auto” for galleries with cropped images
_description:
WordPress added [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2024/10/18/auto-sizes-for-lazy-loaded-images-in-wordpress-6-7/ Auto Sizes for Lazy Loaded Images in WordPress 6.7].

In Galleries that use the setting "Crop images to fit" the images often overlap the box they need to cover by quite a bit (especially when Editors use landscape images in portrait boxes).

Browser heuristics don't seem to be considering the overlapping when calculating which image file to fetch for the layout box.

The result is quite often blurry images in such Galleries.

I'd therefore suggest to remove the "auto" keyword from the sizes attribute of images inside Galleries with the setting "Crop images to fit" enabled (or maybe, instead, when the image orientation does not match that of the layout box).

summary: Toolbar: one search entry point for the admin and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes one search entry point in the Toolbar. The front end gets the same search item the admin has, in the same place and with the same shortcut.

=== Current behavior ===

The Toolbar has two search controls. They share the same icon, but they work in different ways.

 * In the admin, the item sits on the left, after the site name. It shows the icon and the shortcut (⌘K or Ctrl+K) and it opens the command palette.
 * On the front end, the item sits on the far right, after the account item. It is a field that expands on focus and opens the site search results. It has no shortcut.

On small screens the front-end search is hidden, so the Toolbar has no search there.

The field is also the reason the account item is not the last item on the right on the front end. Which create an odd inconsistency. 

[[Image(before-front-toolbar.png)]]

=== Proposal ===

 * Remove the search field from the right side of the front-end Toolbar.
 * Show the same item the admin has, in the same position, with the same icon and shortcut.
 * On the front end, the item and the shortcut open a small dialog with one field: "Search the site". Enter opens the site search results, same as today.
 * In the admin nothing changes. The item opens the command palette. 

[[Image(after-front-toolbar.png)]]

The dialog follows the look of the command palette, so both read as the same control.

[[Image(after-front-search-dialog.png)]]

=== No React, almost no weight ===

This proposal does not bring the command palette to the front end.

The dialog is a native `<dialog>` element with a plain search form. It needs no React and no editor packages. In my prototype it adds around 4 KB for logged-in users. For comparison, loading the command palette on the front end added around 1.6 MB of scripts (uncompressed) in the same test.

The weight was the main concern when the command palette on the front end was discussed before. This approach avoids it.

=== Why ===

 * One mental model. One icon, one place and one shortcut to search, in the admin and on the site.
 * The item does not move. The Toolbar is the only part of the interface that follows the user between the site and the admin. I believe its controls should stay in the same place when the user crosses.
 * The account item becomes the last item on the right in both contexts.
 * More space on the right side, where plugins and hosts add their own items. Same goal as #66157.
 * Search comes back on small screens.
 * Nothing is lost. The search does the same thing it does today.

=== Accessibility ===

 * The same shortcut works in both contexts.
 * The dialog moves focus to the field when it opens. Escape closes it and focus returns to the Toolbar item. The browser handles this natively.
 * The field has a clear name, "Search the site". Today the label is only "Search".
 * The Toolbar keeps its layout on focus. Today the field grows inside it.
 * Without JavaScript, the item can be a plain link to the search page.
 * RTL: no change, the item mirrors as in the admin.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * The search request is the same (`?s=`). Themes and search plugins keep working.
 * Code that removes the search item keeps working, there is nothing to remove.
 * Custom CSS for the old field stops applying.
 * "Search the site" is a new string.

=== Follow-up ===

The command palette could use the same label and offer a "Search the site for …" result. Then both contexts answer the same way. This part lives in Gutenberg, so it needs its own issue.

=== Related ===

 * #65221 has the same goal and keeps the field on the right. This ticket goes one step further.
 * #64672 added the command palette item to the Toolbar.
 * #64875 discusses the position of that item.
 * #26940 is an older proposal for the front-end search.
 * #66157 frees space on the right side.
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/73708 Gutenberg #73708] discussed the command palette on the front end.

summary: Editor: Add a background clip block support to facilitate text gradients
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77141.

Adds a `background.backgroundClip` block support, so a block can set which box its background is painted into: `border-box`, `padding-box`, `content-box`, or the `text` itself. Clipping to the text is what gives blocks a gradient text fill, since CSS has no gradient colour.

For the text value the style engine also emits `-webkit-background-clip` and
`-webkit-text-fill-color`, and the block skips the `has-background` class because
nothing paints the block's background. For the box values only the fill colour
is reset, because `-webkit-background-clip` is an alias of `background-clip` in
Chromium and resetting it would discard the value.

The setting is not part of appearance tools. A theme opts in by setting
`settings.background.backgroundClip`, either true or an array of the values it
wants to offer.

The editor controls and the `core/heading` and `core/paragraph` opt-ins arrive with
the next Gutenberg package update.

summary: Emoji: Consider eliminating expiry-based invalidation of wpEmojiSettingsSupports sessionStorage cache
_description:
Currently the results of the emoji-loader's tests for whether or not emoji are supported get cached in the browser's `sessionStorage` for 1 week. For most users, this expiration will never be reached since the browser tab would be closed and the `sessionStorage` cleared anyway. For the minority of users who keep a single tab open for weeks at a time, including those who restore tabs after installing an OS update, there can be scenarios where (1) the OS or Twemoji was updated to support emoji but the cache causes Twemoji to still be loaded, or (2) the emoji support was not changed and yet the browser re-checks support after a week unnecessarily. 

See [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/4562#discussion_r1243983163 GitHub pull request discussion] for more context and possible solutions.

Nevertheless, as of #58472 the emoji tests have been greatly optimized so the cost of re-calculating support unnecessarily is not a meaningful performance hit, especially since ever since emoji support was introduced until now, the tests were being run on every page load anyway. This may not be worth the effort to resolve.

summary: KSES: Re-implement using HTML API
_description:
Since its initial commit, WordPress has relied on the KSES library to sanitize and normalize and transform content from untrusted sources. Unfortunately, the parsing inside of `wp_kses()` has never been spec-compliant, leading to numerous challenges in safely, efficiently, and reliably fulfilling its purpose.

The HTML API provides a mechanism for structurally interacting with HTML in an efficient manner, and `wp_kses()` should be rewritten to lean on that existing capability.

== Resolves

 - #25851 Large attribute values may crash PCRE patterns and cause content loss.
 - #37698 Global pollution in `wp_kses_split()` calls.
 - #48873 CSS contents are corrupted by `wp_kses()`.
 - #51482 `wp_kses()` turns SCRIPT and STYLE content into renderable text.
 - #52333 `wp_kses()` and HTML disagree on the set of named character references.
 - #58377 Block names with consecutive hyphens are corrupted.
 - #58921 Valid tag names are rejected from the allow-list.
 - #59310 `parse_blocks()` called unnecessarily.
 - #61246 `wp_kses()` un-comments HTML comments.
 - #62024 `wp_kses_post()` incorrectly escapes “<” in attribute values.

=== Potentially resolves

 - #51093 CSS `>` corruption.
 - #56118 Slashes are improperly stripped when exporting data.

== Related

 - #63881 Deprecate `wp_kses_stripslashes()`.
 - #65599 HTML sanitization API implementation.

No way to turn off importing alt text from image XMP metadata
_description:
This is a follow-up to issue #63895.  The fix for that issue created a new `wp_get_image_alttext()` function which parses images for XMP metadata and uses that to populate the alt text for the image.  Currently `wp_get_image_alttext()` is called unconditionally - if you don't want this functionality, there does not appear to be any way to turn it off.  You could use the `wp_read_image_metadata` filter to overwrite the alt text after `wp_get_image_alttext()` has already run, but it would be better to have a way to prevent `wp_get_image_alttext()` from running a bunch of unnecessary code in the first place.

I will submit a pull request to address this.

summary: Display an empty sitemap instead of 404
_description:
The sitemap can be empty when something filters its contents (I do that with The SEO Framework via indexability checks, such as "noindex").

When the sitemap is empty, `WP_Sitemaps::render_sitemaps()` currently bails to a 404. 
I recommend sending an empty sitemap instead.

This change aligns with the user's expectations: They can actually see the sitemap and understand it is empty instead of "not working, eh, where do I start?".

Also, with the change, Google Search Console will say, "Sitemap can be read, but has errors" instead of "Sitemap could not be read". The former is a bit more descriptive of the situation.

summary: Rename default category from uncategorized to general or similar.
_description:
In English language versions of WordPress, the default category is named "Uncategorized" (or "Uncategorised" English variants outside of North America).

As categorising something as uncategorised is a bit of a misnomer, I think it would be good to rename the default category as "General" or similar.
 
Based on a quick [https://www.google.com/search?q=inurl:category/general Google search], renaming the default category to General is relatively common.

Based on another [https://www.google.com/search?q=inurl:category/uncategorized%20%22category%20general%22 Google search], it also appears to be relatively common that WordPress users get stuck with the old `category/uncategorized` URL for the renamed category, presumably for SEO purposes.

While existing WP installs would be stuck with content categorised as uncategorised, I think it would be an improvement to rename the default for new installs.

summary: Introduce a REST API endpoint for sites
_description:
It should be possible to manage sites in a multisite configuration through the REST API.

* List sites: `GET wp/v2/sites/`
* Retrieve a site: `GET wp/v2/sites/<id>`
* Create a site: `POST wp/v2/sites/`
* Update a site: `PUT wp/v2/sites/<id>`
* Delete a site: `DELETE wp/v2/sites/<id>`

Data included in a site object should at least mirror the data available for the site in `wp_blogs`. Additional ideal pieces of data for a site include `blogname`, `blogdescription`, `home`, and `siteurl`. It's possible that creating a new meta table for sites can help developers register meta for inclusion with a site object (See #37923).

Sites should be accessible by default for authenticated users only. Network (global) admins should have access to all sites. Site users should have access to the sites they are members of. The "My Sites" list is a great candidate for exploring how this will work. See #15317.

As of the introduction of `get_sites()` in 4.6.0, retrieving sites is a much better experience. The methods used to create, update, and delete sites in multisite are not as pleasant right now. We should investigate each of these and determine what can be done to streamline the process. The first improvement is probably in creating a site. See #40364.

summary: Improve the admin notices accessibility
_description:
Follow-up to #47656. See also #50442/

The admin notices accessibility has room for improvements.

Currently, all the admin notices are just text printed out on the admin pages. They have no special semantics. There are no mechanisms to inform users some important information is printed on the page other than visuals. There are no methods to navigate directly to admin notices nor established standards on their placement.

This way, users with accessibility needs will likely miss important information, as they may have no clue whether and where these messages are printed out.

Depending whether the admin notices are PHP-generated notices that appear after a page load or JavaScript-generated ones that are "injected" into the DOM, there are ways to improve their accessibility. At the very least, the following improvements should be considered, some of them were mentioned in #47656.


== All notices
- establish standards for the admin notices placement in the page: there should be one, well defined, area where notices are printed out (recommended: after the main H1)
- establish standards for the admin notices content: see the discussion related to the "text prefix" on #47656 and #50442
- the above item should apply to the whole WordPress UI, including the block editor
- "inline" notices (the ones printed out in the middle of the page): make a decision whether to keep them or allow only notices at the top of the page 
- if "inline" notices are kept, explore ways to make them more accessible
- worth considering admin notice should be visually prominent and appear within the initial viewport anyways
- consider the introduction of a dedicated PHP class with methods to get / print admin notices and additional features, also keeping into consideration [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2019/08/05/feature-project-proposal-wp-notify/ the WP Notify project] and the recent [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/06/15/call-for-feedback-wp-notify-v1-requirements-document/ call for feedback on the WP Notify v1 requirements document]

== PHP notices
- prepend to the document title a short text to inform users there are notices and their number: the document title is the first thing screen readers announce after a page load
- the notices should be printed out after the main H1 heading as that's the part of the content with higher chances to be navigated to
- define the page area where notices are printed out with an ARIA role that's also a landmark role, e.g. `complementary` (an `<aside>` element) or other role that is a landmark
- add a new "skip link" after the "Skip to main content" one to allow all keyboard users to jump to the notices area: this skip link should only be printed out when there are notices

== JavaScript notices
- all notices injected in the DOM should have an ARIA role `alert` or `status` depending on their "politeness" level, so that they're automatically announced by screen readers

Any additional suggestion and/or technique to improve the admin notices accessibility is very welcome.

Add content management abilities
_description:
This tracks the addition of get abilities for post types via the Abilities API, enabling AI agents to retrieve posts and pages. Introduces a new Abilities API ability, core/content-query, to retrieve and query post (including custom post types with ability support).

Core currently has core/get-user-info for the current authenticated user only. Agent/workflows use cases need to be able to look up any user when permissions allow it.

It should introduce a show_in_abilities option on register_post_type() to control which post types expose abilities, enabled by default at least for post and page initially.
It should support single-post retrieval by ID and multi-post querying with filters for status, author, etc...

summary: Toolbar: keep plugin-added nodes reachable on every viewport
_description:
== Problem ==
The WordPress admin bar (`#wpadminbar`) crowds quickly at narrow viewports. When several plugins each register a top-level node via `admin_bar_menu`, those nodes collide with the right-side items, get clipped behind the right edge, or stop responding to clicks on mobile widths — exactly the cohort that most needs quick access.
Concretely:
 * At desktop widths between roughly 783px and ~1100px (depending on how many plugin nodes are present), plugin-added top-level nodes start disappearing under the right-side area (`#wp-admin-bar-top-secondary`).
[[Image(overflow-before.png)]]


 * At tablet and mobile widths (≤782px), most plugin-added nodes are hidden by the existing responsive CSS, with no fallback path to reach them.

Today this is treated as a per-plugin problem (each plugin should "be responsive"), but the constraint is structural: the toolbar is a horizontal strip with fixed-width right-side items and an unbounded number of plugin-registered left-side items. No amount of per-plugin CSS recovers a node that has been pushed off-screen by the next plugin in the stack.
Prior related discussion: [ticket:26430], [ticket:22059], [ticket:28983].


== Proposed enhancement ==
Provide a Core-rendered overflow path for plugin-added top-level admin-bar nodes:
 1. At narrow desktop widths, plugin-added top-level nodes that no longer fit overflow into a right-side `'''Plugins'''` dropdown.
 2. At tablet and mobile widths, all plugin-added top-level nodes live under that dropdown unconditionally.
 3. Core-owned nodes (`my-account`, `site-name`, `comments`, `new-content`, `search`, `updates`, `customize`, `edit`, `wp-logo`, `my-sites`, etc.) remain in their current positions.
The dropdown is similar to a standard `WP_Admin_Bar` top-level node with children — **the same nested-menu pattern Multisite already uses for `my-sites`**. I believe no new rendering primitive is required.

[[Image(overflow-after.png)]]

=== Reference implementation ===

A working reference plugin is available at [https://github.com/WordPress/wp-admin-bar-overflow WordPress/wp-admin-bar-overflow] (GPL-2.0+). It implements the full pattern on top of current Core with no Core changes — entirely as an overlay using existing filters — so the user experience can be reviewed today without a build.

'''Easiest way to try it:''' the WordPress Playground demo linked from the repo README boots a preconfigured site in the browser.

'''Recommended way to evaluate it:''' install the plugin on a real WordPress site that already has several plugins registering admin-bar nodes (e.g. Query Monitor, Yoast SEO, WooCommerce, Jetpack, an SEO plugin, a caching plugin). The pattern's value is most visible when the toolbar is genuinely crowded by third-party nodes — that's where the overflow behavior, mirroring, and mobile grouping make the difference between reachable and unreachable plugin UI. Reviewing on a near-empty site understates the problem the ticket is trying to solve.

Architecture, filter API, and host-adapter notes live in the repo's `docs/` directory for anyone evaluating an in-Core implementation.

== Rationale ==
Why this belongs in Core, not (only) a plugin:
 * '''The constraint is structural.''' The toolbar is owned by Core; no individual plugin can know what other plugins have added or how much horizontal space remains. Only Core can arbitrate.
 * '''Mobile parity.''' Today, plugin-added nodes are effectively unreachable on mobile for the majority of WordPress users. Plugins that put critical information in the toolbar (e.g., Query Monitor's error counters, e-commerce order badges) lose that signal on the device class where it's often most useful.
 * '''Backward compatibility for plugin authors.''' Plugins keep registering nodes the same way; original DOM positions and IDs are preserved. No plugin code change is required for the existing behavior to be usable on narrow viewports.

== Backward compatibility ==
Additive. The change introduces a new top-level `plugins` (or similarly-named) admin-bar node owned by Core and adds two filter hooks. Existing plugin registrations via `admin_bar_menu` are not modified. Original nodes remain in the DOM at their registered positions; mirrored entries in the overflow dropdown forward clicks to the originals so click-handlers bound to specific node IDs continue to work.
Sites that prefer the current behavior can opt out via the proposed `admin_bar_overflow_enabled` filter.

== Related tickets ==
 * [ticket:26430] — same problem statement, earlier discussion converged on hiding core links rather than introducing an overflow dropdown.
 * [ticket:22059] — broader "make the admin bar responsive" effort.
 * [ticket:28983] — admin-bar length / wrapping at narrow widths.

summary: Secrets API: encrypted, versioned storage for credentials
_description:
The [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/08/25/proposal-a-secrets-api-for-wordpress-7-2/ Secrets API proposal] is for a core API that stores credentials such as API keys and tokens encrypted at rest, keeps a previous version for rotation, and lets hosts replace the storage through a `secrets.php` drop-in. This ticket covers the 7.2 part: the API itself. The admin screen is deferred to 7.3, as the proposal says. The WP-CLI commands stay in the feature plugin for now, since WP-CLI commands ship as WP-CLI packages rather than in core.

The patch is the `src/` directory of the [https://github.com/ericmann/secrets-api feature plugin], copied without changes, plus the wiring the plugin's bootstrap does today. The plugin has been public since 4 September and is at v0.2.0. The documentation, including every place the code departs from the proposal and why, is at [https://secretsapi.dev/ secretsapi.dev].

This is also the storage #64789 asks for. The Connectors screen from #64730 keeps AI provider API keys as plaintext options, which are visible on `options.php`. Stored through this API, they are encrypted under a key that is not in the database, so a database dump or backup no longer exposes them. Moving Connectors onto `wp_set_secret()` and `wp_get_secret()` can follow once this lands.

=== The patch ===

 * **The API:** 14 new files in `src/wp-includes/`.
   * the public functions
   * `WP_Secret` and `WP_Secret_Version`
   * the provider, store and keyring interfaces, with their default and fail-closed implementations
   * the cipher and the key manager

   `src/wp-admin/includes/secrets-site-health.php` adds three Site Health tests and a debug-information section.
 * **Loading:** `wp-settings.php` loads the API, then loads `wp-content/secrets.php` through a new `wp_load_secrets_dropin()` in `load.php`, just before must-use plugins.
 * **Failing closed:** if the drop-in throws, or sets a provider, store or keyring that does not implement its interface, every Secrets API call returns `WP_Error` for the rest of the request. Nothing falls back to the default provider: a broken drop-in has to read as unreachable, never as "this secret does not exist". See [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0007-fail-closed-on-a-broken-drop-in/ ADR 0007].
 * **Capabilities:** `populate_roles_720()` grants `manage_secrets` to administrators on install, and `upgrade_720()` grants it on upgrade. `manage_network_secrets` joins the other network capabilities in `map_meta_cap()`, so only super admins hold it.
 * **Tests:** the plugin's tests for everything in `src/`, 371 of them, in `tests/phpunit/tests/secrets/`. They come with provider and keyring conformance suites for hosts that write drop-ins.

=== Changes and additions beyond the proposal ===

The proposal names `wp_set_secret()`, `wp_get_secret()`, `wp_delete_secret()`, `wp_import_option_as_secret()`, `WP_Secret`, and `WP_Secret_Version`. Everything below differs from or goes beyond that, and is listed so each item can be reviewed, and rejected, on its own. The reasoning for each is on the linked page.

 * `WP_Secret::reveal()` returns `string|WP_Error`, not `string`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * `wp_retire_secret_version()` and `wp_list_secrets()`: [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/rotation/ rotation], [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/retrieval/ retrieval]
 * Network scope, which the proposal describes without naming functions: `wp_set_network_secret()`, `wp_get_network_secret()`, `wp_delete_network_secret()`, `wp_retire_network_secret_version()`, `wp_list_network_secrets()`. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/network/ network].
 * `wp_secrets_validate_name()`, `wp_secrets_memzero()`, `wp_using_secrets_dropin()`, `wp_secrets_provider_is_writable()`, `wp_secrets_provider_label()`
 * The `wp_secret_changed` action, for auditing, plus `WP_Secret::get_name()` and `WP_Secret::withheld()`
 * The `WP_Secrets_Provider`, `WP_Secrets_Store`, and `WP_Secrets_Keyring` interfaces, and their default and fail-closed implementations. The provider replaced the proposal's two-part drop-in contract after hosts on the proposal thread showed it could not describe how they already deploy. See [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/providers-and-keyrings/ providers and keyrings] and [https://secretsapi.dev/decisions/0001-provider-as-outermost-extension-point/ ADR 0001].
 * Constants: ten `WP_SECRETS_ERROR_*` codes, `WP_SECRETS_RECORD_VERSION`, `WP_SECRETS_MAX_NAME_LENGTH`, `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE`, and `WP_SECRETS_CAP_MANAGE_NETWORK`

The [https://secretsapi.dev/spec/scope/ scope page] has the complete list.

=== Testing ===

 * **In this branch:**
   * `npm run test:php -- --group secrets` passes on single site and multisite (371 tests each).
   * `tests/phpunit/tests/user/capabilities.php` passes with both capabilities added to its inventory.
   * The full single-site suite shows no new failures.
 * **The plugin's CI:** PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.3, each against WordPress latest and trunk, plus a multisite job and a WP-CLI smoke test on PHP 7.4 and 8.3.
 * **Drop-in examples:** the ones in the plugin's `examples/` directory have been run against live AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager, against HashiCorp Vault 2.1.1 (including a sealed server), and against OpenBao 2.7.0.

=== Notes for committers ===

 * `$wp_db_version` is set to a placeholder, 61900, which `upgrade_720()` checks. It needs the real revision number on commit.
 * `wp-tests-config-sample.php` ships placeholder salts, and the default keyring deliberately refuses to derive a key from them. When the salts are placeholders, the test bootstrap therefore defines a fixed `WP_SECRETS_KEY` in the main PHPUnit process. The four tests that exercise the salt-based fallback are skipped in that case.
 * Every new symbol is marked `@since 7.2.0`.

summary: Inconsistency in date setting when changing post status
_description:
In my opinion the behaviour of WP is inconsistent regarding setting the post date when changing a post status draft to published:
– Using single post editing or Quick Edit, the former post date is being restored, while
– the current time is being set to all marked posts when using bulk editing.

This can lead to a misconception with massive impact: Expecting the known behaviour from single post editing also for bulik editing leads to the setting of a false date for quantitives of posts.

This also leads to losing direct access to the original publishing date of each post, which has to be researched using SQL on revisions´ dates in wp_posts for restoring it (this is maybe related to Component:Revisions).

My post on this in https://wordpress.org/support/forum/requests-and-feedback/ has been rejected with recommendation to post this in Trac.

summary: Allow PHPMailer class to be reliably overriden
_description:
The WordPress unit test suite currently overrides the global $phpmailer variable with its own MockMailer class. (See https://core.trac.wordpress.org/browser/trunk/tests/phpunit/includes/bootstrap.php#L48)

This achieves the desired effect, but is potentially unreliable. 

If the global $phpmailer object gets unset, or overridden (For example by a buggy, or otherwise badly behaving plugin), then the code in wp-includes/pluggable.php will create a new instance of PHPMailer without any way for code to override that - see https://core.trac.wordpress.org/browser/trunk/src/wp-includes/pluggable.php#L264

The end result would be that a site that shouldn't be sending emails will potentially become one that will.

Potential patch attached. This includes the change to pluggable.php to filter the object after creation, and addition to the test suite to use it.

summary: Tests: Make PHPUnit data providers public and static

PHPUnit 10 deprecated data providers that are not public and static, and PHPUnit 11 removed support for them. On trunk, about 960 of 1,140 data provider methods are not static, across the 512 files that use `@dataProvider`.

Most need only the `static` keyword. A provider that uses `$this` needs a small rework. PHPUnit 9 accepts static providers, so this can land now.

To keep reviews small, please send one PR per directory, and comment here with the directory you're taking.

summary: Reassess the need for the external-http tests
_description:
Tests in the `external-http` group are flakey because they rely on actual network requests over HTTP. There's no mocking in place. Server errors (HTTP 5XX) and more recently an increase in the frequency of HTTP 429 responses from wordpress.org will cause the tests to fail.

Let's reassess the tests in this group and question exactly what it is that each test is asserting.

As an example, the `Tests_HTTP_Functions::test_head_404()` test performs a HEAD request to a non-existent URL and then verifies that the response is not a `WP_Error` and that the response code is `404`.

What ''exactly'' is this verifying though?

* If it's verifying the correct population of the HTTP response code then that should be handled by test coverage on `WP_HTTP_Requests_Response` and a mocked up `\WpOrg\Requests\Response` instance. No need to perform a real HTTP request.
* If it's verifying specifically that a 404 response doesn't result in a `WP_Error` instance being returned by `wp_remote_*()` then can we do that without performing an actual HTTP request? It should be possible with a test-only transport class which returns a mocked raw HTTP response.

Of course we need to be careful not to remove or reduce coverage where it's needed, but I'm positive we can remove many of the actual HTTP requests from these tests (and move them out of the `external-http` group).

summary: Ability names should support versioning
_description:
We've discussed that versioning an Ability should be done within the name of the Ability instead of a formal concept. That is, an Ability could be named `wp/v1/generate-featured-image` to indicate a version. So if a `wp/v2/generate-featured-image` were created, it would be a different Ability entirely, but conceptually tied to the first — most likely used if the input or output schema changes.

I realized that the regex for validating the Ability name currently enforces the `namespace/ability-name` structure, throwing an error otherwise. We should continue to support this structure, but allow for an optional middle version.

I'm going to call this an enhancement and not a bug since we this is only something we conceptually intended and not something we tell anyone to do at this point.

summary: Add a reusable admin CSS class for destructive actions
_description:
As generally recommended, plugin authors should not use regular buttons for destructive actions, like removing something.

However, while there are standardized classes for buttons in WordPress admin (`button`, `button-primary`, `button-secondary`), a similar standardized class is missing for the destructive link. There are several locations in the admin where such links are displayed, but these are all styled using their individual selectors. Therefore plugin authors who want to use this style must either use one of these selectors (that probably do not fit the use-case at all) or recreate the style manually. Therefore I propose to standardize these style rules for a specific class, for example something like `delete-button` or `delete-link`.

summary: Script Modules API: Allow list of enqueued module data to be exposed
_description:
There's no means for a plugin to fetch a list of registered or enqueued script modules for debugging purposes from the Script Modules API as there is from the existing Scripts Dependencies API.

Most likely the `get_import_map()`, `get_marked_for_enqueue()`, `get_dependencies()`, and `get_versioned_src()` methods of the `WP_Script_Modules` should be made public to facilitate this.

summary: Meta boxes hidden by default
_description: On a new install of WP 7.0, meta boxes are now fully hidden by default. This causes confusion when important parts of the editor for many post types no longer appear until the small "Meta Boxes" bar is clicked.

summary: Connectors: REST API responses on the Connectors screen should be preloaded
_description:
For screenshots and for what this backports, see [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77353 Gutenberg PR].

== What? ==

The Connectors screen (`options-general.php?page=options-connectors-wp-admin`) fires several REST API requests after hydration, delaying the Largest Contentful Paint.

Specifically: `GET /wp/v2/settings` (site entity), `OPTIONS /wp/v2/plugins` (the `canUser( 'create', 'plugin' )` check), a hardcoded `GET /wp/v2/plugins/ai/ai` used by the AI-plugin callout, and one `GET /wp/v2/plugins/<basename>` per registered connector — five sequential round-trips with the default connectors.

== Why? ==

These responses are all trivially knowable at render time on the server, so they should be embedded in the initial HTML via `createPreloadingMiddleware` rather than re-fetched by the client after hydration. This also reduces the number of requests on the server, reducing server load.

=== Measured impact (median LCP over 10 runs) ===

|| '''Scenario''' || '''Trunk''' || '''This PR''' || '''Δ''' ||
|| Fast 4G || 1523 ms || 1150 ms || −373 ms (≈24.5%) ||
|| No throttling || 743 ms || 518 ms || −225 ms (≈30.3%) ||

== How? ==

Adds a `{page-slug}-wp-admin_preload_paths` filter to the `wp-build` `page-wp-admin` template so any generated admin page can register page-specific preload paths. Hooks it in the Connectors loader to preload the five paths listed in '''What?''' above (the existing hardcoded preload in the template only covers the root site fields, not the settings entity the UI actually resolves, so `/wp/v2/settings` is added too).

After the change, none of the connector-related REST requests fire on page load — they are served from the preload middleware.

The two remaining requests come from `@wordpress/core-abilities`, which Gutenberg enqueues on every admin page — out of scope here, but a candidate for similar preloading.

----

To achieve the following, REST API responses for `404 Not Found` need to be served to the preload middleware. This is a follow up to r44123 and r44172.

summary: Move the view mode switcher into screen options for multisite users and sites
_description:

summary: Visually expose the labels of the Media Library 'List view' and 'Grid view' links
_description:
Related: #51006, #50921.

Now that accessible tooltips and toggle tips are in Core, see [62741], I think that's a great opportunity to reconsider those parts of the admin UI that we are most accustomed to and that at first glance we do not consider problematic but in fact may be problematic for some users.

One of the most evident cases is about the 'List view' and 'Grid view' links in the Media Library. 

Those two icon-only links do contain visually hidden screen reader text but that's not sufficient. There should be a _visible_ label for them.

Visible label text should always be preferred.

Some users don't understand icons. Some users need to know the accessible name of a control to be able to issue a voice command. The most accessible web and desktop applications use a combination of icon + visble label to take into account the needs of users with diverse abilities.

When there's a really, really, ''really'' good reason to use only an icon, e.g. because of design constraints that can't be solved otherwise, then exposing the accessible name of such a link by the means of an accessible tooltip is an acceptable compromise. Still, it's a compromise. Always prefer visible text.

In this specific case there are two options:

1. Change the design and add visible label text below the icons.
2. Use the new WordPress accessible tooltips. 

It is worth noting that in their first implementation the new WordPress tooltips only supported button eloments. They are going to be extended to support also links but only for the 'tooltip' pattern, not for the 'toggletip' pattern.

For links, as agreed on the discussion starting at https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/12528#issuecomment-5025167415, the only implementation we'd want to have is the 'tooltip' case. As in: an icon-only link that already has an accessible name and needs to visually expose it by the meqans of a tooltip. 

For these two links, the PHP part in the List view is pretty simple to address. However, the JS part in the Grid view may be a little more comples. Still, visible text is the preferred option so I would like to suggest a design change to start with.

summary: Update message slightly uneven
C2PA information is lost on all generated images (Content Authenticity)
_description:
Since August 2026 the AI Act (2024/1689) demands all AI providers to make AI-generated images to be machine-readable as AI-generated.

There is a de-facto standard arising from the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) which is trying to solve this technical problem.

Unfortunately all those metadata gets stripped for all thumbnail images. Even if we disable this via:

{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'image_strip_meta', '__return_false' );
}}}

You can test this with these online tools:
https://verify.contentauthenticity.org/
https://contentauthenticity.adobe.com/inspect

There is also a CLI tool for it:
https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs/blob/main/cli/README.md

The C2PA specifications can be found here:
https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.3/specs/C2PA_Specification.html

Original EU documents with more details:
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202401689#art_50
https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/code-practice-ai-generated-content

The problem is, that we can't just copy the info to the new images. We need to create new content credentials and reference the original images as parent, as this is an "edit" for the C2PA spec.

Fortunately the EU knows about this general technical problem and allows other ways to declare AI-generation, but maybe in the future we need to have this fixed.

Just a heads up!

summary: Add a filter on wp_insert_user function regarding $user_pass
Application Passwords Expiration
_description:
As a developer, I want the option to set an "expiration" date on Application Passwords so that they aren't able to be used beyond the period of time that I know they'll be used.

=== Use case

I've been working with Application Passwords as a replacement for session cookies in an isomorphic decoupled website. I am generating them programmatically and treating them almost identically to sessions. Because they behave like sessions, I want them to expire. I'm working around this presently by including an expiration timestamp in the Application Password name.

While this feature request would solve that specific use case, I believe this would be a worthwhile addition to Application Passwords to add an option to make them more secure.

summary: Abilities API: Send empty object results as {} to JSON clients
_description:
When an ability returns an empty PHP array and its output schema has `type: object`, clients receive `[]` instead of `{}`. `WP_Ability::execute()` passes output validation, because a PHP array is accepted for `type: object`. The result is then sent as JSON without any change:

 * The REST run endpoint returns it with `rest_ensure_response()`.
 * The AI client wraps it in a `FunctionResponse` for the model.

In both cases, an empty array is encoded as `[]`. This does not match the schema. Strict clients may reject it. Some AI providers also require a tool result to be a JSON object.
   
Example: `core/settings-get` (#64605) returns an empty map when no setting matches. Clients get `[]`, but the output schema promises an object.
  
Core already fixes the same problem for schemas. `wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client()` turns an empty `default` on an object schema into `{}`. There is no matching step for output values.
  
=== Proposal ===
  
Add a helper next to `wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client()`, for example `wp_prepare_json_value_for_client( $value, $schema )`. It turns an empty array into an empty object when the schema has `type: object`. It also walks `properties`, `items`, and `additionalProperties` to handle nested values.

Call it only where the result is sent as JSON:

 * the REST run controller, before `rest_ensure_response()`;
 * the AI client function resolver, before creating the `FunctionResponse`.
  
`WP_Ability::execute()` stays unchanged, so PHP callers still get the value the ability returned. The helper runs after output validation.
   
Open question: how to handle mixed types like `array( 'object', 'null' )`. The suggestion is to convert only when `object` is one of the types.

summary: Feature: Add libvips-based Image Editor to WP Core
_description:
WP 7.1 is taking a big step forward with regards to Media processing with the [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/06/04/call-for-testing-client-side-media-processing/ client-side media processing] effort. I see this as an opportunity make significant improvements to server-side media processing at the same time.

=== Problem: WordPress Media Processing requires excessive server resources

It is common for users to report issues and failures with uploading images (e.g. #23127, #22869, #48522, #55289), and these largely come down to running out of RAM. 

@kirasong confirmed to me recently [https://wordpress.slack.com/archives/C3D6T7F8Q/p1781237448598949?thread_ts=1781029921.088899&cid=C3D6T7F8Q in slack] that:

> image processing has been the highest user of RAM for any individual operation in WordPress for as long as I've been working on the project

Reducing the memory requirements of image processing would improve reliability on resource-constrained hosting environments and allow available memory to be used for serving requests rather than generating image subsizes.

Finally, datacenter CO2 emissions are becoming an increasingly pressing concern. So, WordPress - representing over 40% of the web - needs to endeavour to reduce its server footprint as much as possible.

=== Proposal: Add WP Core support for using [https://www.libvips.org libvips] to process images on the server

Published [https://github.com/libvips/libvips/wiki/Speed-and-memory-use libvips benchmarks] show memory usage and processing times that are often 10–20x lower than ImageMagick and GD. My own testing of libvips for WordPress media uploads has shown improvements in the 5x range for CPU (measuring memory usage seems tricky for Imagick and VIPS, so I don't have figures on hand).

Using libvips in WP Core would result in faster and more reliable uploads, fewer user errors and support/trac tickets, lower memory requirements, reduced hosting costs, lower CO2 emissions, and more. 

We should introduce a new `WP_Image_Editor_Vips` implementation in `wp/wp-includes/class-wp-image-editor-vips.php`, which would use [https://github.com/libvips/php-vips php-vips] to talk to libvips via the php FFI extension. This would be the preferred Image Editor, falling back gracefully to Imagick when libvips is unavailable on the server.  

There is already a [https://github.com/notglossy/vips-image-editor-ffi very capable plugin] that adds such support, but it is largely unknown. Moreover, even if it were to be made a Canonical Plugin, most hosts do not (and won't) support libvips until WP itself supports and educates about it. The core functionality from this plugin could be reviewed, tested and added to WP Core. 


=== Benchmark

See attached SPX profile flamegraphs for uploading the attached large image (on a powerful desktop - 8.6s vs 1.5s. Conversely, the client-side media wasm-vips seems to take around 6 seconds to do the same - and you have to wait on the page while that happens. 

=== Responses to potential objections:
1. "WP 7.1 will have client-side media processing, so server-side media processing is no longer a concern"

This is a fantastic and highly welcome innovation. But it [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/06/04/call-for-testing-client-side-media-processing/#:~:text=System%20and%20Browser%20Requirements only works on] Chromium browsers and in the Gutenberg editor - not the Media Upload tool, nor via plugins from the frontend.  So, plenty of media uploads will still fall through to the backend. 

This effort is ''complementary'' to the client-side media effort (which also uses libvips via `wasm-vips`!).

Also, some sites will surely want to disable the client-side processing, for any number of valid reasons (e.g. battery life, not having to wait for processing to happen before leaving the page)

2. "Very few hosts have libvips installed. So this wouldn't meet the WP Philosophy threshold of core features need to benefit 80% of users"

There's plenty of historical (and current!) precedent for introducing important features that do not meet this threshold.

* The client side media project estimated that [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/74333#issuecomment-4078332777 only a maximum 40% of users] would benefit from it. 
* AVIF support was added despite [https://github.com/WordPress/performance/issues/2519#issuecomment-4716724810 only 30% of hosts supporting it]at the time. 
* And surely many other features and APIs have low initial adoption. 

Hosts' support for libvips is likely to be lower than these precedents, but this is is an opportunity for outreach and education amongst hosts and users - supporting vips is as simple as something like `sudo apt install libvips42 php8.x-ffi`. 

And, again, this would be a progressive enhancement - if your host doesn't support it, WP falls back to Imagick or GD. 

But there is no good reason why this couldn't eventually benefit 100% of WordPress users.

3. "There would be a maintenance burden associated with it"

WordPress already maintains multiple WP_Image_Editor implementations. A Vips implementation would reuse the existing editor abstraction and would likely share much of its behavior with existing editors. The maintenance surface area appears relatively small relative to the potential performance benefits.

Additionally, there's only been a [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commits/trunk/src/wp-includes/class-wp-image-editor-imagick.php couple of commits per year] to the imagick editor.

I and others will surely be willing to help with maintaining this editor.

4. "There are potential security concerns with FFI"

php-vips [https://github.com/libvips/php-vips-ext previously] worked via a .so extension, but that was deprecated in favour of the FFI approach. 

Some hosts disable FFI, but that is a deployment concern rather than a WordPress compatibility concern. For hosts with security concerns, tools such as [https://snuffleupagus.readthedocs.io/ Snuffleupagus] can be used to selectively permit FFI access for libvips while maintaining broader restrictions on FFI usage.

Again, hosts that choose not to enable FFI would continue using Imagick or GD without any change in behavior.

summary: Administration: Avoid $() for selecting with non-literal selectors
_description:
`$( string )` both selects and parses HTML: a string that starts with `<` creates elements instead of selecting them. When the selector is not a string literal, for example a link `href`, `location.hash`, or a value read from the DOM, the caller decides which of the two happens. Escaping it does not help either: a value concatenated into a selector can change what the selector matches.

Prefer `$( document ).find( selector )`, or a narrower context, which only selects, and escape values interpolated into selectors with `$.escapeSelector()`. r64133 made this change for the contextual help tabs in `common.js`; this ticket covers the remaining instances in admin scripts.

summary: Blocks: Add asset file (.asset.php) support for styles in register_block_style_handle()
_description:
In `block.json`, block metadata fields like `style`, `editorStyle`, and `viewStyle` accept file paths via the `file:` prefix (e.g. `"style": "file:./style.css"`). Build tools such as `@wordpress/scripts` and Webpack generate adjacent `.asset.php` files containing automated cache-busting hashes/versions and dependencies.

While `register_block_script_handle()` and `register_block_script_module_id()` detect and load adjacent `.asset.php` files to extract custom handle names, dependencies, and versions, `register_block_style_handle()` previously did not look for an `.asset.php` file, hardcoding dependencies to `array()` and ignoring asset versions or custom handles.

Follows up on Gutenberg issue [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/56838 #56838] (matching the work done for scripts in #60485).

A PR has been prepared with full unit test coverage:
https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14065

summary: GD image editor saves resized indexed PNGs as truecolor (regression since 3.5)
_description:
== Summary ==

This is the GD follow-up to #36477 (see comment:62 and comment:63), where the Imagick side was fixed in [59589].

Since 3.5, the GD editor saves every resized sub-size of an indexed (color type 3) PNG as truecolor RGBA. Sub-sizes are often several times larger than the original.

In 3.4, `image_resize()` did this:

{{{#!php
<?php
if ( IMAGETYPE_PNG == $orig_type && function_exists('imageistruecolor') && !imageistruecolor( $image ) )
	imagetruecolortopalette( $newimage, false, imagecolorstotal( $image ) );
}}}

It checked the original image and converted the new one. [22094] moved this into `WP_Image_Editor_GD::_save()`, which checks the image being saved. `_resize()` always returns a truecolor image from `wp_imagecreatetruecolor()`, so for sub-sizes the check is always false and the conversion never runs.

== Steps to reproduce ==

1. `add_filter( 'wp_image_editors', fn() => array( 'WP_Image_Editor_GD' ) );`
2. Upload `tests/phpunit/data/images/png-tests/cloudflare-status.png`.
3. Check the sub-sizes' PNG color type: all are 6 (RGBA). Expected: 3 (indexed).

== Results ==

Core's png-tests fixtures, trunk editor classes, PHP 8.3, libgd 2.3.3. Percentages are sub-size bytes relative to the original upload, averaged across generated sizes, with the worst single size in brackets.

||= Fixture =||= Transparency =||= Trunk =||= Patched =||
|| cloudflare-status.png || none || 405% (707%) || 110% (189%) ||
|| Palette_icon-or8.png || none || 195% (359%) || 78% (140%) ||
|| test8.png || binary || 261% (413%) || unchanged ||
|| deskcat8.png || partial || 226% (424%) || unchanged ||

Patched output is visually indistinguishable from trunk (PSNR ~39 dB vs. the truecolor output).

== Scope: opaque images only ==

`imagetruecolortopalette()` discards alpha on libgd 2.3.3, even for a minimal two-color image with `imagealphablending( false )` and `imagesavealpha( true )`. Transparent regions become opaque. Preserving transparency would need a per-pixel loop in PHP, which isn't practical on large images. So the patch converts only indexed sources with no transparency, and leaves transparent ones as they are today.

== Proposed patch ==

* In `load()`, record whether the source is palette-based and whether it has any transparency (`imagecolortransparent()` index or non-zero alpha in the palette).
* In `_save()` for `image/png`, when the source was an opaque palette image, convert a copy of the image to a 256-color palette and save that.
* Convert a copy, not `$image` itself: converting in place makes a later WebP/AVIF save from the same editor fail (0-byte file), since GD can't write those from palette images (see performance#2018).
* Unit tests: opaque indexed fixture stays indexed after resize; transparent indexed fixture keeps its alpha; PNG then WebP save from the same editor both succeed.

Related: #36477, #30402, #63448, #53408

summary: Comments: Hide zero-count status filters on the Comments list table
_description:
The Posts list table (`WP_Posts_List_Table::get_views()`) hides any status
filter link — other than "All" — whose post count is zero:

{{{
if ( ! in_array( $status_name, $avail_post_stati, true ) || empty( $num_posts->$status_name ) ) {
	continue;
}
}}}

`WP_Comments_List_Table::get_views()` has no equivalent check. As a result,
"Pending", "Approved", "Spam", "Trash", and "Mine" are always rendered as
filter links above the Comments list table, even when their count is `(0)`.

On a typical site with few or no pending/spam/trashed comments, this clutters
the screen with filter links that lead to an empty list, rather than only
showing filters that are actually useful.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Go to a site where every comment is approved (no pending, spam, or
   trashed comments).
2. Go to Comments in wp-admin.
3. Observe the filter row above the list: "All | Mine | Pending (0) |
   Approved (12) | Spam (0) | Trash (0)".

Expected behavior: filters with a zero count, other than "All", should not
be shown — consistent with how the Posts list table already behaves for
post statuses.

summary: Support for the SameSite cookie attribute
_description:
IETF's [https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-west-first-party-cookies Same-site Cookies draft] was [https://www.chromestatus.com/feature/4672634709082112 shipped in Chrome 51 and Opera 39].

The SameSite cookie attribute instructs a browser not to send that cookie with cross-origin third-party requests (such as iframes, embedded images, and Ajax requests). This effectively mitigates CSRF attacks as, for example, the user will not be authenticated for a given third party URL that's being used in a CSRF attack.

More information on the SameSite attribute can be found here: http://www.sjoerdlangkemper.nl/2016/04/14/preventing-csrf-with-samesite-cookie-attribute/

We should investigate whether setting the `SameSite=lax` attribute is of benefit to the `auth` and/or `logged_in` cookies in WordPress, and if so consider implementing it once the draft becomes an RFC.

PHP uses the `setcookie()` wrapper for setting cookies, which means that setting the SameSite attribute is not possible using that function, until such point that support for the attribute gets added. If WordPress were to implement the SameSite attribute, we'd need our own cookie handling function which constructs and sets the `Set-Cookie` header itself, and use it in place of `setcookie()` (side note: this may also be beneficial to unit testing).
