Implement `ignore-scripts` to harden npm usage
_description:
Lifecycle scripts in npm packages -- in particular `postInstall` scripts -- are a significant security concern because by default they execute automatically for all dependencies.

Running `npm install` or `npm ci` not only installs packages but also runs the `postInstall` script in every direct and transitive dependency in the entire dependency tree. [https://socket.dev/blog/ongoing-supply-chain-attack-targets-crowdstrike-npm-packages The recent "Shai-Hulud" supply chain attack on the npm ecosystem] has been successful in part due to `postInstall` scripts that have allowed it to rapidly self-propagate.

We should strongly consider implementing `ignore-scripts = true` in the `.npmrc` file in order to disable the automatic execution of lifecycle scripts. This will primarily help protect contributors against malicious postInstall scripts that may be introduced by attacks on packages in the dependency tree.

Ironically WordPress core just introduced its own `postInstall` script in #64393. This is far from ideal.

Making this change will cause some short-term pain while we determine the best way to ensure that all dependencies continue to work and/or provide clear instructions for contributors if manual subsequent steps become necessary. As the ecosystem reels from "Shai-Hulud" supply chain attack I fully expect to see more packages remove their postInstall scripts in favour of documenting subsequent steps necessary to, for example, install dependent binaries.

There's some tooling available to assist with determining which dependencies include lifecycle scripts, but not a lot:

- `npm query ':attr(scripts, [postinstall])'`
- `npm query ':attr(scripts, [preinstall])'`
- `npm query ':attr(scripts, [install])'`
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/can-i-ignore-scripts
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lavamoat/allow-scripts

Related links:

- [https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/NPM_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html#3-minimize-attack-surfaces-by-ignoring-run-scripts OWASP recommends using ignore-scripts]
- [https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-10-0-0-blocks-lifecycle-scripts-by-default pnpm since version 10 no longer runs any lifecycle scripts by default]
- [https://www.nodejs-security.com/blog/npm-ignore-scripts-best-practices-as-security-mitigation-for-malicious-packages NPM ignore scripts best practices]

AVIF uploads get JPEG sub-sizes when Imagick (ImageMagick 6) reports the file as HEIC
_description:
Hi everyone,

I searched the existing tickets before posting and didn't find anything that matches this exactly. Related are #53645 (HEIC to JPEG conversion in 6.7) and #62365 (HEIC mapping vs. `image_editor_output_format` overrides), but as far as I can tell they cover real HEIC uploads, not AVIF files. If this is a duplicate, please point me to the right ticket.

== Summary ==

On a server with ImageMagick 6.9.11, uploaded AVIF files get their sub-sizes (thumbnail, medium) generated as JPEG instead of AVIF. The reason seems to be that Imagick identifies the AVIF file as HEIC, so the HEIC to JPEG mapping kicks in.

== Environment ==

 * WordPress 7.1.3, fresh install, no content
 * PHP 8.5.9
 * Imagick 3.8.1 with ImageMagick 6.9.11-60 Q16
 * GD (bundled) with AVIF support
 * Theme: Twenty Twenty-Five

== Is this the latest version? ==

Yes, I tested on a fresh install of 7.1.3.

== Does it happen with all plugins deactivated and a default theme? ==

Yes. The install is new, Twenty Twenty-Five is active and no plugins are active. Debug logging is enabled and nothing is written to the log. `image_editor_output_format` and `image_editor_default_mime_type` have no filters attached.

== Steps to reproduce ==

 1. Use a server where `WP_Image_Editor_Imagick` is selected (ImageMagick 6.9.11, AVIF listed in the supported formats).
 2. Upload an AVIF file to the Media Library.
 3. Look at the attachment metadata (`wp_get_attachment_metadata()`) or the uploads folder.

== Expected result ==

The original stays `image/avif` and the sub-sizes are generated as AVIF (e.g. `image-150x150.avif`).

== Actual result ==

The original is stored as `image/avif`, but the sub-sizes are created as JPEG (`image-150x150.jpg`, `"mime-type": "image/jpeg"` in the metadata).

== What I found when debugging ==

 * `wp_get_image_mime( $file )` returns `image/avif`, and so does `get_post_mime_type()`.
 * `new Imagick( $file )` reports `getImageFormat()` = `HEIC` and `getImageMimeType()` = `image/x-heic` for this AVIF file.
 * After `wp_get_image_editor( $file )`, the editor's `mime_type` property is `image/heic`.
 * Calling `$editor->save( $path, 'image/avif' )` explicitly works fine and writes a valid AVIF. So Imagick can encode AVIF, the problem only occurs in the normal upload flow where no target type is passed.
 * Site Health lists the default transforms `image/heic → image/jpeg` (plus heif and the sequence types).

My guess is that ImageMagick 6 handles AVIF through the libheif delegate and therefore labels it as HEIC. WordPress then seems to take the type from Imagick instead of from the file itself, and the default HEIC to JPEG mapping is applied to what is really an AVIF file. I haven't looked deeper into the code than this, so please correct me if I'm wrong.

== Workaround ==

Forcing GD fixes it, since GD reports the format correctly:

{{{
add_filter( 'wp_image_editors', fn() => [ 'WP_Image_Editor_GD' ] );
}}}

With that filter, new uploads get AVIF sub-sizes after regenerating thumbnails.

== Possible direction ==

Maybe the editor could use the mime type detected from the file (`wp_get_image_mime()`) when Imagick returns a HEIC type for a file that WordPress itself identifies as AVIF. ImageMagick 6.9.11 is old, so this may be an edge case, but it is still shipped by some distributions and hosts.

Thanks for taking a look. I can provide a sample AVIF file and more test output if that helps.

summary: Media Library Search Includes Extra URL Parameters Added After Search
_description:
After using the media library search and the url parameter is set, if an additional parameter is set it doesn't parse just the "search" parameter and instead includes everything after "search=" ignoring any additional "&" and treating it like a string.

I would expect this to pick out just the search parameter to ensure the current search is persisted.

summary: Add core support for random content redirects
_description: WordPress Core does not include functionality to redirect a request to a randomly selected post or page. This behavior is currently implemented through plugins or custom code. This ticket proposes discussing whether a minimal, opt-in core implementation should exist. Any implementation could rely on existing query and rewrite APIs without introducing user-facing settings or defaults. @matt recently mentioned this as something to consider for 7.0 based on his early plugin here: https://wordpress.org/plugins/random-redirect/

summary: Implement WHATWG MIME Sniffing
_description:
WordPress interacts with MIME media types in a number of places in ad-hoc ways. These tend to perform unique parsing, which means they lack consistency and correspondence with how browsers parse MIME types.

For reference, the MIME media type is often derived from the HTTP `Content-Type` header, which contains a type, a subtype, and an optional list of parameters. A common example is `text/html` indicating HTML, `image/png` indicating a PNG image, and `application/xhtml+xml` indicating the XML serialization of HTML.

Discrepancies arise when the supplied type string doesn’t match exactly the anticipated forms. For example, with parameters or whitespaces:

 - `text/html; charset=utf8`
 - `text/plain ;   charset="utf-8;iso-2022-jp`

For reliable, consistent, and secure parsing, WordPress should implement the [https://mimesniff.spec.whatwg.org WHATWG MIME Sniffing specification], which the browsers will implement. This will ensure agreement between the server and clients on what content type strings refer to which media types.

The MIME Sniffing specification governs `Content-Type` values //and also// a limited number of media types from files based on byte sequences in the “resource header” — the first 1445 bytes of the binary data. These binary sniffs are mostly limited to media types relevant to browsers.

== Ad-hoc parsers

 - `wp_finalize_template_enhancement_output_buffer` in `template.php`
 - `wp_mail` in `pluggable.php`
 - Global code in `wp-mail.php`
 - `wp_staticize_emoji_for_email` in `formatting.php`
 - `download_url` in `wp-admin/includes/file.php`
 - `discover_pingback_server_uri` in `comment.php`
 - `do_enclose` in `functions.php`
 - `get_file_extension_by_mime_type` in 

== Related tickets

 - #40175 Inferred MIME types from files inconsistent.
 - #45670 sniffing MIME media types based on different rules than a browser would use

summary: Introduce WHATWG-compliant encoding name canonicalization.
_description:
WordPress largely treats character encoding names in an agnostic fashion, passing them off to browsers, `iconv()`, and `mb_convert_encoding()` transparently. This can lead to confusing data flow for text data, particularly because it’s unclear how arbitrary text coming into WordPress will be handled.

The [https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/ ENCODING spec] defines which character encodings should be supported by web-integrating systems and which variations of each encoding’s name should be treated as equivalent aliases.

For example, while `l1` and `us-ascii` are both treated by browsers as `windows-1252`, they are never recognized as such within WordPress. In fact, since `mb_convert_encoding()` and `iconv()` don’t follow this interoperability standard, they fail for a number of supported encodings.

As WordPress moves towards deprecating non-UTF-8 support (#62172), it should provide robust mechanisms for converting text at the boundaries of input and output to aid this transition.

Prior work normalized UTF-8 detection in #61182, but focused on the detection of `UTF-8` specifically, and without taking into account the additional encodings in the WHATWG standard.

Further work should provide standards-compliant canonicalization while being explicit which set of supported charsets is being detected. For instance, the set of `mysql` charset names is disjoint from the set of web standard charset names.

=== Activities requiring ENCODING support.

 - Decoding full HTML documents.
 - Reading and writing emails.
 - Printing `<meta charset>` tags.
 - Inferring MIME content type.

== Related work

 - #64427 inferring MIME content type.

summary: User Profile: Add option for custom admin color scheme
_description:
Related: #65776

**Task:** Add a new "Custom" option to the Administration Color Scheme setting on the Users > Profile settings page that allows the user to select an accent color and sidebar background color to apply to their WordPress admin interface.

**Context:**

With the [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/07/31/design-system-theming-in-wordpress-7-1/ design system theming color tokens] added in WordPress 7.1, one of the intended next steps from the original [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/07/07/merge-proposal-design-system-theming/ merge proposal] is to explore "Enhanced user customization through theming".

There's a long-term ambition here to enable full configurability for customizing the entire WordPress admin interface, including the content area and "dark mode" themes. There have been [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/42388 some concepts for this] as far back as 2022 and the [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2023/07/12/admin-design/ "Admin Design" phase 3 overview].

What's proposed in this ticket is a smaller, incremental step that enables user customization and builds upon existing support for color schemes and design system theming.

**Design Notes:**

The attached image can give an idea of how it could be integrated into the existing settings. It is not a design proposal (I am not a designer) and I'd welcome design input on a final design.

**Implementation Notes:**

This would likely depend on (be blocked by) API improvements proposed in #65776. 

This should also integrate with site editor improvements in r62454 ([https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/78397 Gutenberg#78397]).

Generated styles for wp-admin interface elements may use parts of [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/theme `@wordpress/theme`], either the ThemeProvider itself (React-based) or [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/theme/src/color-ramps internal color ramp logic], which may require changes in the package to expose this as a generalized JavaScript utility not bound to React.

summary: Toolbar: same W and site name behavior in the admin, the editors and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes two fixed links in the Toolbar. The W always goes to the Dashboard. The site name always goes to the site. Both work the same in the admin, in the editors and on the front end.

It replaces #66235, which covered only the site name.

== Current behavior ==

The W and the site name are the first two items of the Toolbar.

 * A click on the W goes to the About WordPress page. It is the first item of the Toolbar, and it goes to a page people rarely need.
 * A click on the site name changes with the place. In the admin it goes to the site. On the front end it goes to the Dashboard.
 * The site name menu also changes. In the admin it has only Visit Site. On the front end it has Dashboard, Plugins and Themes.
 * When the site has no site icon, the icon changes too. It is a house in the admin and a gauge on the front end.

Since 7.1 the Toolbar is also displayed in the editors. There, the Toolbar has no link to the Dashboard. The W goes to the About page and the site name goes to the site.

== Proposal ==

'''The W'''

 * Click: the W always goes to the Dashboard.
 * Menu: Dashboard is the first item. The other items stay the same.
 * Small screens: the W stays visible. Today it is hidden under 600px.

[[Image(toolbar-w-menu.png)]]

'''The site name'''

 * Click: the site name always goes to the site.
 * Menu: the same items everywhere. Visit Site, Plugins and Themes. On multisite, Manage Site comes right after Visit Site.
 * Icon: the site icon when the site has one, as it works since 7.1. When the site has no site icon, the same default icon everywhere.

[[Image(toolbar-site-name-menu.png)]]

The Dashboard has one place, under the W. It leaves the site name menu.

Small screens:

[[Image(toolbar-small-screens.png)]]

== Why ==

 * The W gets a useful click. The logo in the top left corner is the most visible item of the Toolbar. I believe people expect it to go to the home of the admin. About WordPress is still in the menu, one click away.
 * The W menu keeps its role. It still holds the links about WordPress. Only the click changes.
 * One click to the Dashboard from everywhere. This matters most in the editors, where the Toolbar has no way back to the Dashboard today.
 * One behavior to learn. Each item does one thing. People don't need to check where they are before they click.
 * Two clear places. The W is the admin and the site name is the site. Today one item switches between both.
 * It works on multisite. My Sites stays next to the W, as today. In the Network Admin, the W goes to the network Dashboard.
 * **Better on touch screens**. A tap on the site name opens the menu. Today, in the admin, that menu has a single item.

== Accessibility ==

 * The accessible name of the W becomes "Dashboard". Today it is "About WordPress". The name says where the link goes.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change.
 * Both menus have the same items in the same order everywhere. It is more predictable for screen reader users.
 * The site icon is decorative. The site name stays next to it.

== Backward compatibility ==

 * Two clicks change. The W goes to the Dashboard and not to the About page. On the front end, the site name goes to the site and not to the Dashboard.
 * The Dashboard item moves from the site name menu to the W menu. It keeps its ID.
 * People only see the items they have access to, same as today.
 * Classic themes keep their extra items (Widgets, Menus, Background and Header) after Themes.
 * The other menu items keep their IDs. Plugins that add items to these menus keep working.
 * Under 600px the Toolbar gets one more item, the W.

== Related ==

 * #66235 is the first version of this proposal, only for the site name. I will close it in favor of this ticket.
 * #28398 and #19184 asked for fixed links years ago and were closed. Since then, the site name got the site icon and the Toolbar is displayed in the editors.
 * #65088 site icon in the Toolbar.
 * #65091 Toolbar in the Site Editor and Block Editor.

summary: Cross-origin isolation: crossorigin attribute is mis-scoped for <source> elements
_description:
Editing a post in the block editor dies with a PHP fatal error and a blank white
screen. The failure is inside core's own cross-origin isolation output buffer.

{{{
PHP Fatal error:  WP_HTML_Tag_Processor::apply_attributes_updates():
Cannot use output buffering in output buffering display handlers
in /wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php on line 2644
}}}



The reported function name alternates between `substr()` (line 2639) and
`WP_HTML_Tag_Processor::apply_attributes_updates()` (line 2644) across requests —
both are inside the same method.

== Environment ==

 * WordPress 7.1
 * PHP 8.x
 * Browser: Chromium 137+ (Chrome/Edge). '''Does not reproduce in Firefox or Safari.'''
 * User with `upload_files` capability
 * `memory_limit = 1024M`, peak usage at time of failure ~180 MB — not a memory issue

== Steps to reproduce ==

 1. Run WordPress 7.1 with client-side media processing enabled (the default).
 2. Open `/wp-admin/post.php?post=<id>&action=edit` in '''Chromium 137 or newer'''.
 3. Ensure the rendered admin page contains at least one '''cross-origin''' resource
    (`<script src>`, `<link href>`, `<audio src>`, `<video src|poster>`, `<source src>`)
    whose URL starts with neither `site_url()` nor `/`.

A minimal way to guarantee condition 3 in a test install:

{{{#!php
<?php
add_action( 'admin_enqueue_scripts', function () {
	wp_enqueue_script( 'repro-external', 'https://example.com/repro.js', array(), null, false );
} );
}}}

'''Expected:''' the editor loads.
'''Actual:''' blank page, fatal error above, no output at all.

== Why it looks intermittent ==

Two independent gates make this bug appear random, which cost us a long
bisection through 27 plugins before we found it:

 1. '''Browser gate.''' `wp_start_cross_origin_isolation_output_buffer()` returns
    early for anything below Chromium 137, so the same site is fine in Firefox.
 2. '''Content gate.''' `wp_add_crossorigin_attributes()` only calls
    `set_attribute()` for cross-origin URLs. With no such resource on the page,
    `$lexical_updates` stays empty and `apply_attributes_updates()` returns at
    its first line — never reaching the failing statements. So one post edits
    fine while another, containing an embed or an external script, fatals.

== Code path ==

Hooks —
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/default-filters.php#L699-L702 default-filters.php:699-702]:

{{{#!php
<?php
add_action( 'load-post.php', 'wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation' );
add_action( 'load-post-new.php', 'wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation' );
add_action( 'load-site-editor.php', 'wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation' );
add_action( 'load-widgets.php', 'wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation' );
}}}

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/media.php#L6646 media.php:6646]
`wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation()` gates on the feature flag, screen and
`upload_files`, then calls —

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/media.php#L6701 media.php:6701]
`wp_start_cross_origin_isolation_output_buffer()`, which opens an '''output
buffering display handler''':

{{{#!php
<?php
ob_start(
	static function ( string $output ): string {
		header( 'Document-Isolation-Policy: isolate-and-credentialless' );
		return wp_add_crossorigin_attributes( $output );
	}
);
}}}

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/media.php#L6725 media.php:6725]
`wp_add_crossorigin_attributes()` runs `WP_HTML_Tag_Processor` over the whole
buffered document '''from inside that handler''', and for `AUDIO`/`VIDEO`/`SOURCE`
additionally uses bookmarks and `seek()`.

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L2605 class-wp-html-tag-processor.php:2605]
`apply_attributes_updates()` is where PHP raises the error, at
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L2639 line 2639]
and
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L2644 line 2644]:

{{{#!php
<?php
$output_buffer       .= substr( $this->html, $bytes_already_copied, $diff->start - $bytes_already_copied );
$output_buffer       .= $diff->text;
$bytes_already_copied = $diff->start + $diff->length;
// ...
$this->html = $output_buffer . substr( $this->html, $bytes_already_copied );
}}}

It is reached from
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L4912 get_updated_html():4912]
and also from
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L2717 seek():2717],
which flushes pending updates mid-parse at
[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1/src/wp-includes/html-api/class-wp-html-tag-processor.php#L2746 line 2746].

Note the local variable in `apply_attributes_updates()` is named `$output_buffer`
but is a plain string — the class contains '''zero''' `ob_*` calls (verified by grep
over the whole file). The PHP error is the output-buffer lock error surfacing
while core's own display handler is running; determining the precise trigger is
left to core, but the conflict is entirely within core code.

== What was ruled out ==

Diagnosed on a live install with an instrumented mu-plugin that logs
`ob_get_status( true )` at every hook and dumps a backtrace plus the callback list
of every in-flight hook when a non-default handler appears.

 * '''Not a plugin.''' A disk scan of 39,071 PHP files across all plugins,
   mu-plugins and both themes found no `ob_start()` with a closure in any '''active'''
   plugin. Every third-party handler found uses an array or string callback, so it
   would appear as `Class::method` in `ob_get_status()`, not `Closure::__invoke`.
 * '''Not memory.''' 180 MB used against a 1024 MB limit at the moment of failure.
 * '''Not a drop-in.''' `wp-content/` contains no `advanced-cache.php`,
   `object-cache.php` or `db.php`.
 * '''Confirmed as core.''' `ob_get_status( true )` reports
   `Closure::__invoke [level 0, flags 113]`, appearing between the `user_has_cap`
   and `acf/validate_setting` hook dispatches, inside the `load-post.php` dispatch —
   exactly where `wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation` is registered, and it is the
   first callback on that hook, ahead of every plugin.

== Workaround ==

The documented feature gate disables it:

{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'wp_client_side_media_processing_enabled', '__return_false' );
}}}

This also disables client-side (WebAssembly) media processing, since that is what
the isolation exists for. Using `remove_action()` on `wp_set_up_cross_origin_isolation`
is worse: it leaves the feature enabled while removing the isolation it depends on.

== Suggested direction ==

Any of these would remove the class of failure:

 * Do the tag rewriting '''outside''' the display handler — collect the output with a
   plain `ob_start()` and post-process after the buffer is closed.
 * Send `Document-Isolation-Policy` via the normal headers path and add
   `crossorigin` attributes through `script_loader_tag` / `style_loader_tag`
   filters instead of rewriting the finished document.
 * If the buffer must stay, guard the handler so a failure inside it returns the
   original `$output` unchanged rather than taking the whole screen down.

summary: Theme installer: Themes can be previewed even when the Preview button is disabled
_description:
In the Theme installer at `wp-admin/theme-install.php` the action buttons for the themes that can't be previewed, for example because they are incompatible with the current WP version or the current PHP version, are disabled.

This is intentional to prevent users from installing / activating / previewing an incompatible theme.

However, clicking on any part of the Theme card outside of the buttons still gives access to the Theme preview (note that the Preview and the Live Preview are two different things).

This is unexpected and should be fixed.

To reproduce, the quick way:
- In `src/wp-includes/functions.php` make the two functions `is_wp_version_compatible()` and `is_php_version_compatible()` return `false` early.
- Go to the Theme installer.
- Observe the theme cards have their buttons disabled. The button labels are for example: Cannot Install / Preview, Cannot Activate / Live Preview.
- For a non-installed theme (one that shows the Cannot Install / Preview buttons) click on any part of the theme's card outside of the buttons.
- Observe it brings you to the Theme preview.
- For an installed theme (one that has the Cannot Activate / Live Preview buttons), click on any part of the theme's card outside of the buttons.
- Observe it brings you to the Theme preview.

So for both installed and non-installed theme shown in the Theme installer, clicking the theme's card still gives access to the theme's Preview.

summary: Alternate views for WP List Tables
_description:
Currently, the WP List Table supports two views: default and "excerpts". This distinction is confusing and doesn't easily allow for other differences between the two views.

As a way to create more flexibility in WP List Tables, we'd like to implement mechanisms for users to choose different views, similar to what's found in Gmail, e.g.: Compact, Default, Comfortable. 

This would give us a lot more flexibility in being able to resolve issues where conflicts arise between design, space, and accessibility, because we could offer views where everything is spelled out in a spacious way and also views where information is more compact. As long as the user is able to choose a persistent view that gives them all the information they need, the alternate views can use designs that disclose less detail. 

Example tickets that would be impacted include:

#48751
#32170
#35391

summary: Toolbar: Increase the height to 48 pixels for both desktop and mobile
_description:
Related: #65091, #65849, #65445.

Historically, the toolbar (the admin bar) height has always been 32 pixels and then adjusted to 46 pixels in the responsive view.


This point was recently discussed in the context of the various changes for the Toolbar in WordPress 7.1 and some contributors from the accessibility team pointed out the 32 pixels height appears to be too small for today's average displays and DPI.

The limited height makes hard adding some good focus style.
Also, themes (for the front end) and plugins (for the admin) are forced to take the variable height in account and provide their own styles for the desktop and responsive view, especially when they used fixed / sticky toolbars.

By increasing the toolbar height and making always the same for both desktop and mobile:
- the CSS would greatly simplified
- there would be more space for additional styling e.g. the focus style
- readability would improve
- work for theme and plugin authors would be greatly simplified
- it is also worth noting thet right now a `mobile` CSS class is added to the body (and used to style the toolbar) on the PHP side when the device in use is detected to be a mobile device. This is done via the `wp_is_mobile()` function and this part could be entirely removed.

== Backward compatibility

Many themes and plugins are unmaintained and this should be taken into account. Id' be in favor of considering any sort of opt-in mechanism, for example a theme support of any other kind of flag for plugins and themes. This needs to be considered carefully.

summary: Toggle tips should also display tooltips
_description:
With no visible text label, a toggle tip needs to also display a tooltip to expose its accessible name.

This was deemed a nice to have in #51006, but not critical for initial implementation, as it adds significant complexity.

summary: Remove widget accessibility mode
_description:
With the introduction of the new block editing experience for widgets management, WordPress will have four separate interfaces for managing widgets: block editing, customizer, classic widgets, and accessbility mode.

The accessibility team would like to explore merging the characteristics that accessibility mode uses for better accessibility into the classic widget screen, to cut down to only three modes of operation for widgets.

This will require identifying the characteristics of accessibility mode and finding ways to reproduce those characteristics within the existing widget UI.

The key differences that are obvious are:

1) Use of a text link to 'Add' or 'Edit'
2) Links target each widget via a URL to manage independently.
3) Selection options to choose which sidebar and position will be used for a widget.

These characteristics allow a single widget to be edited in isolation, the ability to assign a location without drag and drop, and visible text tools for handling widgets. 

One possibility to explore is having an add/edit option that opens a given widget in a modal that includes the location selection tools provided in accessibility mode.

summary: Remove the admin menu auto-fold feature & move responsive viewport trigger to 960px.
_description:
Since slightly before the dawn of time (definitely before r20749, but hard to pin down exactly when), the admin menu has automatically collapsed to a reduced width icon-only display on small viewports.

Originally, this occurred on viewports smaller than 900px; later that was expanded to be below 960px. 

When the responsive state of the admin menu was introduced in WordPress 3.8 as part of the MP6 redesign, the scope of the auto-fold behavior was limited to between 782px and 960px.

On today's devices, those widths only occur in a handful of limited scenarios: intentionally narrowed viewports, iPad Air in portrait mode, and smaller iPad Pro devices in portrait mode are the primary cases.

The collapsed menu can still be useful for some users, and this is not proposing to remove the ability to fold the menu; but the automatic folding behavior is now obsolete.

This proposal is limited to removing the behavior that automatically triggers a folded menu & to move the trigger for the responsive menu to happen at 960px.

This would help resolve issues like #46307, in that this menu would only ever appear if a user has explicitly made the choice to use it, and they would be able to change that choice if they needed clarification on a specific item in the menu. Right now, if you are inside that narrow viewport range, your only option for the menu is a version that has no visible labels at the top level and can be difficult to understand.

summary: In WP Admin -> Posts add 'Filter by author' dropdown
_description:
In  the posts view, I think it would be an enhancement to have an additional 'filter by author' dropdown.

[originally also address adding visible labels, being addressed in #63971]

summary: Improve and extend focus styles for Windows High Contrast mode
_description:
See [44544] and #41286.

[44544] introduced new focus styles for the Windows High Contrast mode only for the main user interface elements like buttons, links, media views elements.

In order to cover all the controls in the admin, there's the need to explore the admin parts that make use of uncommon styles or don't inherit the relevant CSS, for example the Customizer, the themes browser, etc.

Some thorough testing on Windows would be greatly appreciated.

summary: Improve the focus state in the admin bar
_description:
The default focus state in the admin bar is very subtle. It's visually very similar to the focus state used for submenus in the side menu.

As indicated by #64859, this state makes the user experience somewhat confusing. In my opinion, this confusion is caused mostly because the focus state is different from other top level contexts, and doesn't clearly convey what is actually going on. 

The focus state in the adminbar should be made stronger - either by using the same focus state used in the side menu (inverted colors in blue/white) or by using the same focus state used in the main content area (outlined).

Given the context, the inverted colors makes more sense.

summary: Real time collboration effectively disables persistent post caches while anyone edits a post
_description:
When real time collaboration is enabled, any time the post editor is open the persistent caching for `WP_Query` is effectively turned off due to the frequent updates to the `wp_sync_awareness` meta key.

Any time post data is updated, the post's `last_changed` time up updated in persistent caches to indicate the entire `WP_Query` (and various other post caches) need to be invalidated.

To reproduce:

1. Configure a site with a persistent cache
2. Enable real time collaboration
3. Without an editor open, run the WP CLI command `wp eval "var_dump( wp_cache_get_last_changed( 'posts' ) );"` a couple of times, a few seconds apart
4. Observe that the value does not change between calls.
5. Edit a post, any post type will work.
6. run the WP CLI command `wp eval "var_dump( wp_cache_get_last_changed( 'posts' ) );"` a couple of times, a second apart
7. Observe that the value does changes every second

As objects cached in the `post-queries` group use the outcome of `wp_cache_get_last_changed( 'posts' )` to salt their caches, this means that leaving the editor open will effectively prevent the caching of post queries throughout the site.

Reducing the frequency the `wp_sync_awareness` meta data is updated will reduce the severity of the problem, if that's possible. 

To an extent this is an inevitable effect whenever the RTC syncing data is stored in the post and post meta tables, ideally it would be limited to only occur when an edit is made so that leaving a browser tab open doesn't have negative implications on the performance of a site.

I've put this on the 7.0 milestone for the purposes of investigating the issue to see if mitigation is option.

summary: Media: add an opt-in filter to generate animated image sub-sizes
_description:
== Background ==

Resized versions of animated GIFs have always lost their animation: both GD and Imagick flatten animated images when resizing. This is the subject of #28474, open since 2014. It stalled server-side because GD cannot preserve frames at all, Imagick is only available to a subset of hosts, and per-frame re-encoding is costly on shared server CPU.

Client-side media processing (see #64804) changes that calculus. Image decoding, scaling, and encoding happen in the uploading user's browser via wasm-vips, which is available regardless of host configuration and can decode and re-encode every frame of an animated image. The cost is paid once, by the uploader, rather than on the server.

Animated re-encodes are still expensive (roughly 10-20 seconds for a very large GIF even with tuned encoder settings), so this should not be the default. It is proposed as a developer opt-in.

== Proposal ==

Add a new filter, `wp_generate_animated_image_subsizes` (boolean, default `false`):

{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'wp_generate_animated_image_subsizes', '__return_true' );
}}}

The filtered value is exposed on the REST API index as `animated_image_subsizes`, inside the existing client-side media processing block in `WP_REST_Server::get_index()` (alongside `image_sizes` and `image_size_threshold`, only for users who can `upload_files`). The client-side pipeline reads it from there and, when enabled, keeps the animation in uncropped sub-sizes of animated GIFs instead of flattening them to the first frame.

Behavior details:

 * Only uncropped sub-sizes (`medium`, `medium_large`, `large`, uncropped theme sizes) keep their animation. Cropped sizes such as `thumbnail` are always generated from the first frame; per-frame smart-cropping is out of scope.
 * The filter name says "animated image" rather than "GIF" deliberately: the client pipeline can also preserve frames for animated WebP, and APNG has come up on #28474. The initial implementation is exercised with GIFs.
 * Server-side uploads still produce static sub-sizes; the filter currently only affects the client-side path. If server-side animated resizing (per #28474) ever lands for Imagick, the same filter can control it, which is why it is proposed in core rather than as an editor-only setting.
 * `wp_calculate_image_srcset()` already declines to mix the full-size animated GIF with its sub-sizes in one `srcset`. With animated sub-sizes that guard becomes overly conservative but harmless; relaxing it can be a follow-up.

== Implementation ==

The client-side consumption (editor settings plumbing, upload pipeline, and the vips worker restoring the all-frames load path with tuned GIF encoder settings) ships via the Gutenberg package updates in [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/80385 Gutenberg PR #80385] (see [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/80383 Gutenberg issue #80383] for the full design discussion, including the encoder tuning that makes the opt-in cost reasonable).

The core-side change is small: apply the new filter in `WP_REST_Server::get_index()`, expose the value on the index, and add the field to the block editor preload field lists in `wp-admin/edit-form-blocks.php` and `wp-admin/site-editor.php` (these must stay in sync with `packages/core-data/src/entities.js` for preloading to work).

Core PR: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/12572]

== Related ==

 * #28474 - WordPress destroys animation in animated GIF when it resizes (this provides an opt-in resolution for editor uploads via the client-side path, as proposed in [https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/28474#comment:58 comment 58])
 * #64804 - Client-side media processing

After uploading a plugin that "requires" other plugins, the "Activate Plugin" button leads to a wp_die() WSOD
_description:
When a plugin is installed by uploading a zip, the result screen always shows an "Activate Plugin" button, even when the plugin's `Requires Plugins` header lists plugins that are not installed or not active. Clicking it takes the user to a bare `wp_die()` white screen with no admin menu and no way forward other than the browser's back button or the "Manage plugins" link.

[[Image()]]

The Plugins list table and the AJAX install flow already block activation in this case (the AJAX flow since #61294). The installer screen should behave the same way.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Create a plugin with this header and zip it:

{{{
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Dep Test Plugin
 * Requires Plugins: classic-editor
 */
}}}

2. Make sure the required plugin (Classic Editor in this example) is not installed on the site
3. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and install the zip.
4. On the result screen, click "Activate Plugin".

**Actual result:** a `wp_die()` white screen reading "Error: Dep Test Plugin requires 1 plugin to be installed and activated: Classic Editor. Manage plugins."

**Expected result:** the result screen does not offer "Activate Plugin" (or "Network Activate" on multisite) and tells the user which plugins are missing, inside the normal admin screen.

== Cause

Uploads and non-JS installs run through `update.php?action=upload-plugin` and `update.php?action=install-plugin`, which render `Plugin_Installer_Skin`. `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` builds the activate links based only on the install result, the `activate_plugin` capability and whether the plugin is already active. It never checks the plugin's requirements, and `update.php` never initializes `WP_Plugin_Dependencies`.

The link goes to `plugins.php?action=activate`, where `activate_plugin()` calls `validate_plugin_requirements()`, gets a `plugin_missing_dependencies` error, and `plugins.php` passes it to `wp_die()`.

== Proposed fix

In `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()`, when the install succeeded and the user can activate the plugin, call `validate_plugin_requirements()`, the same check `activate_plugin()` runs. If it returns a `WP_Error`, remove the activate and network activate links and show the error message as an admin notice.

`validate_plugin_requirements()` already calls `WP_Plugin_Dependencies::initialize()`, and `Plugin_Upgrader::install()` has already cleared the plugins cache, so the newly installed plugin's header is read correctly. Reusing this function also means the installer screen never offers a link that `activate_plugin()` would reject, including the WordPress and PHP version checks and the `validate_plugin_requirements` filter.

Patch attached.

== Testing instructions

1. Apply the patch.
2. Repeat the steps to reproduce above.
3. Confirm the result screen shows an error notice naming the missing plugin and no "Activate Plugin" button.
4. Upload a plugin without a `Requires Plugins` header and confirm "Activate Plugin" still appears.
5. Optional: repeat on multisite from Network Admin and confirm "Network Activate" is hidden only in the unmet-dependency case.

== Related

* #61294: the same bug in the AJAX install flow, fixed in 6.5.4 by adding a missed `initialize()` call.
* #64493: improving plugin dependency messages (7.2).
* #22316: the original Plugin Dependencies feature, shipped in 6.5.

summary: Notes: Restore child notes trashed along with their parent note
_description:
Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84100

When a top-level note is trashed, `wp_trash_comment()` also trashes its child notes. However, `wp_untrash_comment()` has no counterpart for this: when the parent note is restored, its child notes stay in the trash.

To fix this, `wp_untrash_comment()` needs a counterpart to the child-trashing logic in `wp_trash_comment()`. The approach can follow the precedent of [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/2bf0714531e2d478640ccb46fe5463a092530ac4/src/wp-includes/post.php#L4351-L4356 wp_trash_post_comments()] / [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/2bf0714531e2d478640ccb46fe5463a092530ac4/src/wp-includes/post.php#L4412-L4429 wp_untrash_post_comments()]:

* When a top-level note is trashed, store the IDs of the child notes that are not yet in the trash (i.e. the ones being trashed along with the parent) in the parent note's `_wp_trash_meta_children` meta.
* When the parent note is untrashed, restore only the recorded child notes that are still in the trash, then delete the meta.

Importantly, a child note the user trashed individually before trashing the parent should **not** be restored when the parent is trashed and then restored. The parent's trash/untrash cycle should only undo what it did itself.

summary: Toolbar: free horizontal space on the right side
_description:
This ticket proposes to make the account menu item narrower, so the right side of the Toolbar has more space. The panel underneath stays the same.

=== Current behavior ===

The account item on the right side of the Toolbar is the widest text element in the bar. It shows a full sentence with the display name, plus the avatar.

The right side is also where plugins and hosts add their own items (notifications, site status, account links). As more items land there, the space gets tight. Long display names and long translations make it tighter.

On small screens Core already reduces this item to the avatar only. So the bar works well with a narrower account item.

=== Proposal ===

Show only the display name and the avatar in the bar. The ful l sentence moves inside the panel, next to the avatar, the username and the profile links.

[[Image(toolbar-proposed-crop.png)]]

=== Why ===

 * More space on the right side. The account item gets around 50px narrower in English and more in many languages. That space goes to the items that need it.
 * Clearer control. I believe the name and the avatar are enough to read as "your account". It is the same pattern used by most products.
 * Better fit for long names and long translations. Less truncation and wrapping in the bar.
 * Consistent with small screens, where Core already narrows this item.

=== Accessibility ===

 * The accessible name of the account control becomes the display name. Shorter and clearer for screen reader users.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change. Same menu, same items.
 * The full sentence is still available to everyone who opens the panel.
 * RTL: no change, the text mirrors as today.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * Existing strings and translations stay in place.
 * Node IDs and the menu structure stay the same. Plugins that add items to the account panel keep working.
 * Sites that customize the account item text with the `gettext` filter keep working.

=== Related ===

 * #48894 improvements to the account panel.
 * #61615 crowding on the right side of the Toolbar.

summary: TypeScript code quality improvements for 7.2
_description:
This is the JavaScript analog to the PHP in #65817, but using TypeScript instead of PHPStan. Adding TypeScript checking will likely identify bugs that need to be fixed along the way and it will greatly improve the resilience of the codebase against defects being introduced in the future, either by humans or by agents.

This follows the introduction of the TypeScript in the core codebase in #64662. The initial files being checked with TypeScript are those used by the Code Editor, the tooltip logic, and some build tooling, as is listed in [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/7.1.0/tsconfig.json#L29-L37 tsconfig.json]: 

{{{
"src/js/_enqueues/lib/codemirror/htmlhint-kses.js",
"src/js/_enqueues/lib/codemirror/javascript-lint.js",
"src/js/_enqueues/wp/code-editor.js",
"src/js/_enqueues/wp/wp-tooltip.js",
"tools/gutenberg/copy.js",
"tools/gutenberg/download.js",
"tools/gutenberg/utils.js"
}}}

This list needs to expand so that TypeScript checking can eventually cover the entire JS codebase. 

TypeScript can be invoked via `npm run typecheck:js`. Note also the related command do check JSDoc: `npm run lint:jsdoc`.

Note that while PHPStan has the concept of [https://phpstan.org/user-guide/baseline the baseline] which allows adopting static analysis for an existing codebase with errors, this is not available for TypeScript. So this means we'll need to either go file-by-file adding TypeScript checking with the existing config, or make the existing config (or separate configs) much looser and then stricter over time. 

This will naturally be closely related to improvements to JS documentation across the codebase:

- #65951 (Fix all the JSDocs)
- #65860 (General docblock improvements for 7.2)
- #40831 (Customize: Further improve JS inline documentation)

summary: State Styles: Scope per-instance rules to the block's root element
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/83986.
Related: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/83925

Fixes per-instance state styles on blocks whose root selector starts with another block's class. List Item registers `.wp-block-list > li`, and the instance class that scopes a state rule sits on the `li` itself, so swapping the leading compound for that class produced `.wp-states-xxxx > li`, which matches nothing. A breakpoint value set on a list item was written to the stylesheet but never applied.

The fix keeps a leading compound that names a different block as an ancestor and puts the instance class on the block's own compound, giving `.wp-block-list > .wp-states-xxxx`. A leading compound followed by a `wp-block-*` class still describes a nested element, as in `.wp-block-button .wp-block-button__link`, so those selectors keep the existing behaviour.

summary: Stop concatenating scripts and stylesheets in wp-admin and retire load-scripts.php and load-styles.php
_description:
This functionality was added 14 years ago, #8628. At the time it made the loading of wp-admin quite faster by reducing the number of HTTP requests by more than 50%. The downside is that each wp-admin page has it's own set of concatenated scripts and stylesheets making them harder for caching in browser/network caches. Nevertheless the benefits of the reduced number of requests was greater than the insufficient caching.

This changed when HTTP/2 became more popular. Scripts and stylesheets are loaded much more efficiently there and concatenation is generally not needed. This allows for better browser/network caching and for eventual prioritization. In that terms disabling concatenation of scripts and stylesheets in wp-admin would reduce complexity and improve performance in many cases.

summary: Default Navigation fallback menu title is ambiguous and produces a redundant accessible name
_description:
== Description

On a fresh WordPress site using a block theme, when there is no existing Navigation Menu or suitable Classic Menu, {{{WP_Navigation_Fallback::create_default_fallback()}}} creates a published {{{wp_navigation}}} post titled “Navigation”:

{{{#!php
'post_title' => _x( 'Navigation', 'Title of a Navigation menu' ),
'post_name'  => 'navigation',
}}}

Source: [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/class-wp-navigation-fallback.php#L270-L284 class-wp-navigation-fallback.php]

This causes two related problems:

1. In the Site Editor, “Navigation” is both the name of the Navigation screen and the title of the default menu. The generic menu title does not distinguish the menu from the screen or describe the menu's purpose.
2. The Navigation post title is also used as the frontend navigation landmark's accessible name when the block has no explicit {{{ariaLabel}}}. {{{WP_Navigation_Block_Renderer::get_navigation_name()}}} returns the post title, which is then output as the {{{aria-label}}} on the {{{<nav>}}} element.

Relevant code:

* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/blocks/navigation.php#L583-L605 get_navigation_name()]
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/blocks/navigation.php#L907-L919 aria-label output]

The resulting markup includes:

{{{
<nav class="wp-block-navigation …" aria-label="Navigation">
}}}

Because the {{{<nav>}}} element already exposes the navigation landmark role, assistive technology may announce this as “Navigation, navigation.” The label is redundant rather than meaningfully distinguishing this landmark from other navigation landmarks.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Start with a fresh WordPress installation using a block theme, with no existing {{{wp_navigation}}} posts or Classic Menus.
2. Open the Site Editor and access the Navigation screen, causing the default fallback Navigation Menu to be created.
3. Observe that the menu is titled “Navigation,” the same name used for the screen.
4. View the site frontend and inspect the Navigation block's {{{<nav>}}} element.
5. Observe {{{aria-label="Navigation"}}}.

== Expected result

The generated menu should have a meaningful administrative title that distinguishes it from the Navigation screen, and the frontend navigation landmark should have a meaningful, non-redundant accessible name.

One possible approach would be to name the administrative object “Primary", which would use “Primary” as the accessible label. 

== Actual result

The generated menu is titled “Navigation,” which is ambiguous in the editor and becomes a redundant accessible name on the frontend.

== Related issues

* #47123 established that navigation landmark labels should not include the word “Navigation,” because screen readers already announce the landmark role.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/59706 Gutenberg #59706] tracks the broader need for meaningful and unique Navigation Menu names and notes that automatically generated names are currently inadequate.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/52488 Gutenberg #52488] tracks broader improvements to Navigation fallback behavior.

summary: REST API: rest_filter_response_fields() fatals on PHP 8 when response data is stdClass (e.g. /wp/v2/taxonomies?type=…&_fields=…)
_description:
On PHP 8+, requesting a taxonomy collection with _fields can fatal instead of returning a trimmed JSON response.

rest_filter_response_fields() passes response data into _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive(), which calls array_intersect_key() without ensuring the value is an array. When WP_REST_Response::get_data() is a stdClass (seen with /wp/v2/taxonomies?type={post_type}&_fields=…), PHP throws:

TypeError: array_intersect_key(): Argument #1 ($array) must be of type array, stdClass given
in wp-includes/rest-api.php (_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
Related: for slug-keyed collections such as /wp/v2/taxonomies and /wp/v2/types, _fields intersects top-level keys (taxonomy/type slugs) with field names (name, slug, …), so a successful response is often an empty array [] even when taxonomies exist. Filtering should be applied per item in the collection.

== Steps to reproduce
Site on PHP 8.0+ with at least one public custom post type that has a REST-visible taxonomy (e.g. CPT UI testimonial + testimonial_category), or any setup that yields object-shaped taxonomy collection data for a type filter.
While logged in (or with sufficient caps), open or request:
GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?type=testimonial&_fields=name,slug,rest_base,hierarchical,types
(Substitute any post type slug that has associated taxonomies.)

Observe HTTP 500 and the TypeError above in the error log.
Also compare:

`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies`
`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?_fields=name,slug,types,rest_base`

The second often returns [] even though the first returns a non-empty object keyed by taxonomy slug.

== Expected behavior
No fatal.
_fields returns a trimmed representation of each taxonomy in the collection.
Non-array response data is coerced to an array (or skipped) before array_intersect_key().
Actual behavior
Uncaught TypeError in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() when data is stdClass.

== Environment
WordPress 6.x / 7.x (reproduced with current rest_filter_response_fields / _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
PHP 8.x (strict types on array_intersect_key())
Triggered from the block editor / CPT UI (User-Agent: node) hitting the taxonomies endpoint after editing a CPT
Code pointer
wp-includes/rest-api.php:

rest_filter_response_fields()
_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() — assumes $array1 is always an array
rest_api_default_filters() re-registers rest_filter_response_fields on rest_api_init.

== Suggested fix
Guard/coerce in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() / rest_filter_response_fields():

{{{#!php
<?php
if ( is_object( $data ) ) {
    $data = get_object_vars( $data ); // or recursive array cast
}
if ( ! is_array( $data ) ) {
    return $response;
}
}}}

For non-numeric collections whose values are arrays/objects and whose keys are not in the _fields list, apply _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() to each item (same idea as the wp_is_numeric_array() branch).

summary: Connectors API: a documented connector type for AI services the AI Client does not drive
_description:
`WP_Connector_Registry::register()` documents one value for `type`, `ai_provider`, which is special-cased: the key is handed to the PHP AI Client and validated on save, and reset when validation fails (https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13031 describes the re-validation). A non-generative AI service, one that returns probabilities and confidence rather than text, cannot pass that validation, so registering it as `ai_provider` would clear a working key.

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/64791 established that plugin-defined types are intended (its use cases include "add a non-AI connector"), and that works: registering under a type of one's own renders the card in its own group on Settings › Connectors, the key is stored and masked by core, and it resolves with the usual env/constant/option precedence. Two gaps remain:

 1. The `register()` docblock still reads as if `ai_provider` were the vocabulary: `@type string $type Required. The connector type, e.g. 'ai_provider'.` Nothing states that other values are supported or how the Connectors screen treats them.

 2. An AI service outside the AI Client is neither `ai_provider` nor a plain non-AI service, and there is no name for it. Each such plugin invents a type, and the screen groups by type, so two judgement-model connectors from two authors would land under two headings. A documented core value (`ai_service`, or whatever name fits) would let them group together, and would give the AI plugin something to recognise when it decides whether AI credentials exist.

Ask: document that plugin-defined types are supported, and add or name one for AI services the AI Client does not drive.

Working example: https://github.com/juanlentino/jev-connector, registered as `ai_decision`, verified on 7.1. Companion request on the PHP AI Client side, for a capability that would let such models be first-class there: https://github.com/WordPress/php-ai-client/issues/296.

summary: Remove login test cookie.
_description:
Follow up to r6009 for #2039.

The year is 2007, the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browser_wars#Second_browser_war_(2004%E2%80%932017) second browser war] is in its early days and has ten years to run; the most popular social media network is Myspace and WordPress introduces a test cookie the login screen because cookies can not be presumed to be available.

The year is 2027, browsers now work together for [https://wpt.fyi/interop-2026 Interoperability], social media is fractured, and -- significantly for this ticket -- **first party cookies can be presumed to be available**.

My proposal is to remove the test cookie from the login screen. Many CDNs are configured to bypass caching for cookies prefixed `wordpress_` or `wp_`, although the smarter ones ignore `wordpress_test_cookie`.

An alternative to removing the test cookie entirely is to provide a filter to allow for it to be enabled by developers if required. If this is the preferred option I suggest the filter be opt-in rather than opt-out.

summary: Admin: Button styles are not consistent in active-while-focused states
_description:
r46241 (#34904) added styles which remove the focus ring while a button is active by assigning {{{box-shadow: none}}} to {{{.button:active}}}. This effect can be seen when activating buttons like "Search Posts" on the Posts screen.

**Bug:** Not all buttons apply this consistently, for example the "Save Changes" button on the Settings > General screen maintains the focus ring while active.

**Technical Analysis:**

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L84 Secondary buttons] and [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L52 buttons forced active with the .active class] hide the focus ring, while [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L32-L36 plain (primary) buttons] and [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L119-L123 tertiary buttons] have no corresponding style. These styles are used in generating color scheme stylesheets that are loaded after the base styles from {{{buttons.css}}}, and take priority over the base styles.

**Resolution:**

Adding {{{box-shadow: none}}} consistently to all of the button mixins would likely be the expected resolution given the current state of button styling.

In parallel, Gutenberg's [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/84090 GB#84090] discusses general styling updates for this state which may ultimately make current assumptions obsolete, but does not block consistency improvements in the meantime.

summary: Taxonomy: Repeated hierarchy decoding slows hierarchical term queries
_description:
get_term_children() calls _get_term_hierarchy() at each recursive step. The hierarchy option may already be in the object cache, but get_option() still unserializes the complete map on every read. WP_Term_Query's hierarchical hide_empty pass repeats the traversal for each empty parent.

This can make ordinary category lists slow even when SQL is cheap. A local fixture with 8,000 terms in a balanced tree (up to four children per parent, empty parents and nonempty leaves) needed 12,182 hierarchy reads to build one list. Only two SQL queries were executed. The fixture has one published post assigned to the leaves of each taxonomy; it is a controlled fixture rather than a production-site measurement.

PHP 8.3.0, MariaDB 11.4, OPcache enabled in both versions. Medians of five alternating runs:

|| Operation || Terms || Before || After ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 1,000 || 0.116 s || 0.030 s ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 4,000 || 1.706 s || 0.131 s ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 8,000 || 6.909 s || 0.227 s ||
|| WP_Query including descendants || 8,000 || 1.269 s || 0.152 s ||

The option cache was warmed before timing. Each measurement used a fresh PHP process, so the term-query result cache was cold. WordPress bootstrap was excluded from the timer. List HTML, returned terms and post IDs matched between versions in all 90 measurements.

To reproduce the path, create a sizeable hierarchical taxonomy with empty parents and posts assigned to its leaves, then time these calls in separate requests without a pre-existing term-query result cache:

{{{#!php
$start = microtime( true );
$html = wp_list_categories( array(
    'taxonomy' => 'category',
    'echo' => false,
    'title_li' => '',
) );
$elapsed = microtime( true ) - $start;
}}}

The proposed change passes an already loaded hierarchy into the existing descendant traversal and reuses that hierarchy within the hide_empty pass, keyed by taxonomy. No persistent or request-global cache is introduced. A warm term-query result cache bypasses the affected hide_empty processing, so the same gain should not be expected on cache hits.

Eight regression tests cover ordering, invalid taxonomies, leaves, insertion/reparenting/deletion between calls, descendants excluded from the result set, multiple taxonomies and hierarchy read counts. All eight pass with the patch; the two read-count tests fail without it. The broader term, category and query/taxQuery groups complete 753 tests and 1,933 assertions with no failures. One pre-existing PHPUnit warning also appears on the original code; strict --fail-on-warning runs exit nonzero.

Compatibility point for review: option filters are called fewer times. A get_term callback that changes hierarchy relationships during the same hide_empty pass may observe the pass's existing hierarchy snapshot. Changes between separate calls are covered by tests.

summary: Block Hooks: Skip parsing and re-serializing post content in the_content when no blocks are hooked
_description:
Pages with a lot of block content are slow because, since 6.8, every the_content call parses and re-serializes the whole post even when no block is hooked, and the per-block Block Hooks visitors run on top of that.

[58291] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/b39f58ec3eab0f2b66dccebbf0fc97baaaaa9a15 b39f58ec]) returned early from apply_block_hooks_to_content() when nothing was hooked.
[59101] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/2952e563aae229fe497e723996cc5a58b92e1401 2952e563], #61902) removed that early return so template parts still get the theme attribute. Parsing and serializing now always run, and the has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) check only selects the visitors ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1171 blocks.php:1171]).
[60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/e800c60ec09a06cf73407f992d7ed1352e3c3973 e800c60e], #63287, in 6.8.1) added a temporary hooked_block_types filter inside apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1354-L1356 blocks.php:1354-1356]). That filter makes the has_filter() check always true on this path, so the per-block visitors always run.
The PRs for [60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8695 8695], [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8700 8700]) do not mention this, and it appears to be unintended.

Timing apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() on ~1 MB of block markup with nothing hooked (PHP 8.4):

trunk: 34-35 ms per call
with the patch: 0.4 ms per call
=== Steps to reproduce ===

In the PHPUnit test environment on trunk [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06 0004f4d2], with no plugins and no hooked blocks, create a post with ~1 MB of nested paragraph, group and columns blocks.
Time repeated calls of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object( $post->post_content, $post ).
Expected: the content is not parsed when nothing is hooked. Actual: it is parsed and re-serialized on every call.
=== Proposed fix ===

Return the content unchanged at the top of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object(), before the temporary filter is added, when:

get_hooked_blocks() is empty and has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) is false;
has_block( 'core/template-part', $content ) is false;
$ignored_hooked_blocks_at_root is null (REST passes an empty array, which keeps the full path, #65008).
Output is unchanged for well-formed content. Content with a stray closing delimiter renders as it did before 6.8. (Since 6.8, the temporary wrapper block has been making the parser recover and render those broken blocks anyway, and the patch removes that recovery whenever it skips the pass.)

The patch adds one test, test_apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object_returns_content_unchanged_if_no_hooked_blocks, to applyBlockHooksToContentFromPostObject.php. Run with php vendor/bin/phpunit --group block-hooks (SQLite).

AI disclosure:
AI assistance: Yes
Tool(s): Claude Code, Codex CLI
Model(s): Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra
Used for: root-cause analysis, git history checks, patch, test and benchmark drafting, accuracy review; 
I reviewed the patch and the claims.

Unlimited query for invalid post names
_description:
In case a request which is being parsed as one which sets a "name" query var (eg.: `http://localhost/wordpress-latest/2016/11/08/[` ) includes an invalid name ( the `[` ), a query without any limit with empty post_name is triggered:

{{{#!sql
SELECT wp_posts.*
FROM wp_posts 
WHERE 1=1 
AND ( ( YEAR( wp_posts.post_date ) = 2016
AND MONTH( wp_posts.post_date ) = 11
AND DAYOFMONTH( wp_posts.post_date ) = 8 ) )
AND wp_posts.post_name = ''
AND wp_posts.post_type = 'post' 
ORDER BY wp_posts.post_date DESC
}}}

The problem with the query is that it matches all the drafts in the database, since they don't have the post_name set (is empty). This may have a performance implications for the database in case it contains a lot of drafts (or posts without the post_name set for any reason) as it queries all the posts.

The `post_name` is being set as empty due to `sanitize_title_for_query` in https://core.trac.wordpress.org/browser/tags/4.6.1/src/wp-includes/query.php#L2717

I have tested a more suitable validation function than `trim` ( eg.: `sanitize_title` ) in https://core.trac.wordpress.org/browser/tags/4.6.1/src/wp-includes/query.php#L1609 but it leads to archives being served on those invalid URLs, which does not seem like good fix.

Trying to set `posts_per_page` to 1 in case the `name` is parsed based on the rewrite rule (which seems like a good thing since we really should be interested in a single and unique post_name in such cases) hits a wall as the is_singular() returns true and the limit is not set even if the posts_per_page is present ( due to https://core.trac.wordpress.org/browser/tags/4.6.1/src/wp-includes/query.php#L3215 ).

So the fix might need to be more complicated than.

summary: Support structured color options for wp_admin_css_color
_description:
Related Gutenberg issue: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/80766

**Request:** [https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_admin_css_color/ `wp_admin_css_color`] should accept options for structured color values that can be used by WordPress itself to apply a color scheme without need for stylesheet overrides, and these options should be exposed on the user REST API endpoint when the associated color scheme is selected.

**Background:**

In its current state, `wp_admin_css_color` is largely concerned with providing a stylesheet be loaded associated with a color scheme of a given name. The color scheme itself is applied through the stylesheet targeting specific elements on WordPress pages. While the function accepts an array of `$colors`, those are only used in presenting an option on the user profile page for selecting the color scheme itself, and have no other purpose. They are an unordered, non-semantic set of colors that should not be inferred to carry any meaning in how they should apply to different elements of the admin experience.

WordPress 7.1 will include an [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/07/31/design-system-theming-in-wordpress-7-1/ initial theming implementation], including a new ThemeProvider component that accepts `primary` and `background` theme colors. In WordPress, this is already used to [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/78397 apply the user's color scheme to the Site Editor]. But since these seed values can only be known ahead of time for the default WordPress color schemes, it does not support custom color schemes registered through `wp_admin_css_color`.

**Technical Notes:**

I included a [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/80766#issuecomment-5105493067 comment on the associated Gutenberg GitHub issue] which describes how I think this could be implemented:

In my mind, we could overload `wp_admin_css_color` so it could be called like this:


{{{#!php
wp_admin_css_color( 'ectoplasm', __( 'Ectoplasm' ), [
  'primary' => '#646c3e',
  'background' => '#4f386e',
] );
}}}

`$args` as an array third argument helps support optionality of arguments and future growth. Relatively straight-forward to overload with backwards-compatibility by checking the whether the third argument is a string or array.

Current `$colors` and `$icon` arguments could be inferred from primary/background, or optionally provided explicitly with `'colors'` and `'icon'` to override. Same with `$url` being an optional argument `'url'`.

Since we'd be applying theme colors dynamically to some parts of the admin, a plugin author may not care to provide their own stylesheet and `$url` is optional.

Twenty Fourteen/Thirteen/Twelve Navbar submenu behaviour
_description:
As you all may know, both 2014/13/12 themes require you to hover over a menu item in order to access the submenu item. This isn't a problem for desktops but for touchscreen devices this may pose a problem.

I notice this problem has largely been addressed at least for the 2013 and 2012 themes for Android, iOS and Windows Phone devices (see https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/24767#comment:35). However, on my Windows 8 tablet, it still registers the first tap as a click on both Internet Explorer 11 and Mozilla Firefox (Google Chrome works fine). I believe both browsers somehow do not declare whether the device is a touchscreen.

In addition, for the 2014 theme, the (partial) fix isn't even implemented (I don't know how it got implemented for both 2013 and 2012 themes but was overlooked for 2014), therefore you will still find it hard to click on sub-menus if you're using an Android device.

As for the 2013 and 2012 themes, I know that the Windows 8 tablet userbase is comparatively small, but I believe it will grow over the years. I'm not sure how this can be fixed in the mean time (since the hover/click behaviour seems to rely on a touchscreen detection), but I would like to suggest the following:

- In the Twenty Fifteen theme, this issue seems to be fixed once and for all, as the dropbox arrow next to the menu item is a separate link. Clicking on the arrow itself will maximise/minimise the sub-menu, instead of linking you to the menu item itself.

- However, the Twenty Fifteen theme's menu is only available at the side, instead of the top.

- Thus, if the improvements made in the Twenty Fifteen theme could be backported to Fourteen, Thirteen and Twelve. It would be great!


P.S. I'm not sure what to classify this ticket under, but I guess I will leave it as a 'bug' since the hover and click issues have not been completely addressed, especially on the Twenty Fourteen theme. The same behaviour occurs on WordPress 4.0.1 and 4.1 RC.

summary: Bump minimum PHP version to 8.*
_description:
This ticket tracks discussion and work on the next bump to the minimum PHP version to v8.0 or higher.


== Policy / Criteria for Version Bumps (by @justlevine)

There is **no official policy or criteria** [[https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/58719#comment:30|(ref)]] for handling PHP Version bumps. Pending [[https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/58719#comment:1|that discussion]], the following is based on the processes used until now:

1. Matt is the ultimate decision maker on whether to bump the minimum PHP version.
2. That discussion is initiated by the release/project leads based on several (public and private) factors.
3. A **general** litmus test to gauge whether a version should be bumped is if the % of users (via https://wordpress.org/about/stats/) left behind by the bump is `< 5%`.
4. However, usage stats alone are not reason to bump the minimum PHP Version but also have a positive impact on the project/codebase/tooling/etc.

**Important:** Bumping the minimum PHP version (this ticket) is not the same as changing the [[https://wordpress.org/about/requirements/|minimum ''recommended'' version]] (v8.3 as of 10 Jan 2026).

Background: #62622, #58719, #51043, #57345


== Data Points
Since many years @samiamnot has monthly put the stats updates in comments of the old tickets - see backgroound above. We can continue on this ticket with tracking the appropriate data.

The Stats projection page of @johnbillion [[https://johnbillion.github.io/wp-stats/php.html|can be found here]].

**Note**: .org Stats do not offer a cross-reference between WP/PHP versions. As such these percentages include sites that may already be (colloquially) abandoned on a previous WordPress release,but could theoretically upgrade if their plugin/theme stack supports recent WP versions.

Bumping the minimum version to v8.0 would allow us to remove a lot PHP 7.* compatibility code. The work for this release could be bigger then usual so we should communicate early for when this is planned to be set.


== Projection
This could take quite some time to get below the 5% threshold. Currently as of January 2026 it sits on 22.1%. We'll see how fast it can come down.

An important comment in my view from @jrf about the big effort in maintaining WP running PHP cross-version see #58719. Hopefully we can find some other supportive measures to make users more aware that an upgrade is needed - but thats for another ticket. For the moment lets keep discussions here on how to get to 8.0 and have a space to track usage by @samiamnot 


== Previously
#62622 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.4 in WordPress 7.0
#58719 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.2 in WordPress 6.6
#57345 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 7.0 in WordPress 6.3
#46594 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 5.6 in WordPress 5.2
#16917 Bumping the minimum PHP version to 5.2 in WordPress 3.2
